2ff572f400793d283d2529893efbac34369098a2.summary: arXiv:2611.28025v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Co-creating layouts such as websites and slides is a useful testbed for evaluating multi-turn instruction following of LLM systems. Since an intended layout's appearance cannot be well expressed in a single turn, the user must wait for the LLM to generate a layout then iteratively refine it with the LLM over multiple turns. We present a small-scale, exploratory (n=6) study of this multi-turn process to compare the differences of human-AI and AI-AI teams on the same layout-generation task. Given a reference wire-frame layout, a participant or a language model 'speaker' issues natural-language instructions to a fixed 'listener' LLM over multiple turns until the speaker is satisfied. Rather than an LLM as the judge, we fit a scoring function over geometric layout features using curated human preference data (n=19). We find that LLMs tend to encode the entire layout in the first turn, while humans iterate over many turns on average, writing much shorter instructions. We also find that human-AI teams consistently scored lower than AI-AI teams. This gap is driven by a limiter of human participants in specifying precise sizes and positions (e.g. 42 pixels to the right). Humans perform almost at par with language models on other features like ordering the elements into nested structures. We then perform interventions on the speaker LLMs to make them more human-like, and find it difficult. This raises the challenge of using LLMs as user models to evaluate multi-turn co-creation tasks.
2ff572f400793d283d2529893efbac34369098a2.title: Measuring Human-AI and AI-AI Teams in Multi-turn Layout Creation

3045f765621b56fbc04d8592ad8e7281c46f6d45.summary: arXiv:2611.27673v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hy-MT3 is the third generation of the Hunyuan multilingual translation model family, including \textbf{Hy-MT3-1.8B}, \textbf{Hy-MT3-7B} and \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (MoE)}. Compared with Hy-MT2, Hy-MT3 translates \textbf{more accurately, more completely and more faithfully to user constraints}: on real-world scenario data, the share of samples with mistranslations is reduced by \textbf{43\%}, omissions or additions by \textbf{74\%}, and instruction-following errors by \textbf{40\%}, while language coverage is expanded from \textbf{38 to 102} languages. With only 3B activated parameters, \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models in non-thinking mode}, including flagship models such as Qwen3.8-Max, Kimi-K3.1-Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and approaches the strongest closed-source thinking models such as GPT-6.1-Sol and Gemini-4-Argon, while surpassing models that consume \textbf{more than 30$\times$} its inference compute. Beyond general translation, Hy-MT3 is optimized for two industrial scenarios. For \textbf{game localization}, built with high-quality game-domain data and a professional evaluation system from the Honor of Kings team, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B matches or outperforms strong closed-source models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro on all core metrics, and can be plugged into game development pipelines through an open-source toolchain. For \textbf{image translation}, Hy-MT3 improves context understanding and error correction to better tolerate OCR errors, achieving the best result among models of comparable size. Finally, we open-source \textbf{TransRubric}, a rubric-based automatic evaluation suite for translation, which outperforms other evaluation schemes on the WMT26 metrics shared task test set and is more stable with respect to human evaluation.
3045f765621b56fbc04d8592ad8e7281c46f6d45.title: Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and Practical Multilingual Translation Models in the Wild

30584d8fcc95bb0a9730015cfc2caab66f9ab29a.summary: arXiv:2610.16117v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.
30584d8fcc95bb0a9730015cfc2caab66f9ab29a.title: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues

30bd632113bb2d6225404f21a3b7572005a05a34.summary: arXiv:2611.30179v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sustained lunar-base operations require robots that restore equipment and deliver cargo under conditions unforeseen before deployment. Flown space autonomy executes pre-validated procedures and enters a safe hold outside their scope, whereas foundation models synthesize plans on site that cannot be verified before execution. We formulate these operations as safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued physical evidence, and costly, deadline-constrained sensing. We propose asymmetric knowledge-level replanning (AKR), which treats the planner as an untrusted black box: reversible actions run on the planner's assumptions, and irreversible actions run only after a minimum-cost sensing cover verifies every precondition. Under sound measurements, no irreversible action executes on a false precondition for any planner or record, the sensing cost before an irreversible action is bounded below for every sound knowledge-based policy, and execution with a complete planner ends in a verified goal or a certified hold. AKR executed no hazardous action in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials with sound observations or in 58 full-stack runs; the FF-Replan acting rule executed one in 7% of those trials. The median AKR run took 1.10 times the fastest run on the same mission, against 1.50 under the K-replanner acting rule. AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model; the original PLEXIL and EUROPA$\rightarrow$PLEXIL procedures completed none.
30bd632113bb2d6225404f21a3b7572005a05a34.title: Trustworthy agentic lunar robotics: safety-constrained contingent planning with a foundation-model planner

30f76239188a02820d0d40b5612fe81fe09d3c3e.title: Show HN: New AI edits images based on text instructions

30f910ea65bbf9669faf108e584b6dc62f4cc725.summary: arXiv:2611.29942v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.
30f910ea65bbf9669faf108e584b6dc62f4cc725.title: LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration

31665164906b5e021b2b89f39266078c2ec2df81.summary: arXiv:2611.31051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.
31665164906b5e021b2b89f39266078c2ec2df81.title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation

3180bce5017f79175ce11af34b2d275ff4ae4568.summary: arXiv:2611.29014v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.
3180bce5017f79175ce11af34b2d275ff4ae4568.title: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models

319fa4f46308b2a7b0f380d6e365e6855a9920d1.summary: arXiv:2611.29750v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.
319fa4f46308b2a7b0f380d6e365e6855a9920d1.title: Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement

320b1a5d5b94db83508f28b7ea09984ff87ebd6a.summary: arXiv:2611.29989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: We developed an interpretable workflow linking paired differential proteomics, sparse logistic regression, SHAP attribution, and first-order logic (FOL) rule learning in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Methods: We analysed 213 CPTAC-LUAD tissue samples (111 tumour, 102 adjacent-normal) from 111 patients, including 102 matched pairs. Protein effect estimation and testing used the same complete pairs, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Sparse logistic regression used five-fold stratified patient-grouped nested cross-validation. Preprocessing and model selection were confined to training data, with feature selection repeated within inner folds. A separate five-fold patient-grouped evaluation tested SHAP-guided inductive logic programming (FOL/ILP) using training-derived evidence and discretisation. Results: Quality control retained 9,518 proteins. At FDR below 0.05 and an absolute mean paired log-ratio difference of at least 1, 378 were differentially abundant (40 increased, 338 decreased). The sparse classifier yielded ROC-AUC 0.9997, average precision 0.9998, accuracy 0.9906, and balanced accuracy 0.9906. FOL/ILP yielded held-out accuracy 0.9765, balanced accuracy 0.9767, precision 0.9818, recall 0.9730, and F1 0.9774. HSPA12B, PALM2-AKAP2, STARD13, and PPM1F had non-zero coefficients in all five classifier folds. The most frequent Horn clause occurred in two of five folds. All others occurred once. Conclusions: The workflow connects proteomic classification, attribution, and symbolic rules. Performance reflects tumour-versus-adjacent-normal discrimination within one cohort. Biomarker and clinical claims require independent validation, repeated assessment of rule stability, and further biological annotation.
320b1a5d5b94db83508f28b7ea09984ff87ebd6a.title: Differential Proteomics to XAI Rules: A SHAP-FOL-ILP Modeling for Lung Adenocarcinoma

320d289bb72ec93bddadb87eab53445ec91685fb.summary: arXiv:2611.28820v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Construction site defect analysis increasingly requires linking field evidence to the correct BIM object, because a crack, spalling area, missing sleeve or misaligned support is useful for quality control only when it is connected with component identity, location, responsibility and design intent. This paper proposes a PointNeXt Adapter improved model for BIM component defect association under construction images and design model attributes. The method aligns site image crops, local point cloud patches, BIM component identifiers, geometry attributes, material categories, installation stage, inspection distance, viewpoint quality and source reliability tags into component level inspection windows. PointNeXt learns local geometry and deviation from as built point evidence, while the adapter injects BIM attributes so the same geometric irregularity can be interpreted differently for structural, envelope, MEP and embedded components. The fusion head outputs component link, defect class, defect probability, confidence, dominant evidence and recommended review action. A synthetic multisource BIM inspection dataset is used to evaluate repeated layouts, occlusion, sparse point clouds, registration errors and unseen component arrangements. Results show that attribute aware point learning improves association accuracy, defect recall and confidence calibration compared with image only, point only, simple fusion and adapter free baselines. The framework is positioned as traceable BIM issue review support, requiring manual confirmation and staged field validation before operational deployment.
320d289bb72ec93bddadb87eab53445ec91685fb.title: PointNeXt Adapter Improved Model for BIM Component Defect Association under Construction Images and Design Model Attributes

322ef4f140b31c4cddbfdd27c6c5e754c25514a9.summary: arXiv:2611.30965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.
322ef4f140b31c4cddbfdd27c6c5e754c25514a9.title: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time

323d564846d7d1d9f03d55823964c5c85d0dece1.summary: arXiv:2611.11334v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.
323d564846d7d1d9f03d55823964c5c85d0dece1.title: MoT3DVG: A Benchmark for Outdoor 3D Visual Grounding with Motion-Aware Descriptions and Temporal Cues

32921a09d12a4cf945a2dfae71a95af2547865b2.summary: arXiv:2611.30281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B--14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining \emph{Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs)}, and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.
32921a09d12a4cf945a2dfae71a95af2547865b2.title: Learning Heterogeneous Reasoning in Large Language Models: From Mode Compatibility to Local Bottlenecks

32abca7d21a2ddbfe4dbabf2fce898b7874b064a.summary: arXiv:2609.34113v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding where and why Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents fail is essential for building more reliable systems, yet current evaluation relies on step accuracy, a metric that treats each screen independently and overlooks the underlying structure of GUI environments. This leads to two critical blind spots: (1) functionally equivalent screens are evaluated in isolation, obscuring systematic failure patterns across shared screens; and (2) the long-tailed GUI distribution renders failures on rare but critical screens invisible under standard metrics. To address these issues, we propose \textbf{GUITAR}, a state-centric diagnostic framework that performs structured failure analysis over both states and transitions, using a State Transition Graph (STG) by mapping visually diverse screens to shared functional states. Across 8 agents and 6 tasks from AndroidControl and Mind2Web, GUITAR reveals that 60.4\% of failures occur in 20\% of states, localizing errors to a small set of bottlenecks. Bottleneck-targeted guidance improves SR by 2.8\% and retains a 1.88\% average gain across 7 agents under three-fold trajectory-held-out evaluation with fully automatic STGs. These findings demonstrate the diagnostic and actionable value of structure-aware evaluation within the evaluated mobile and web tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/sqzhang-lazy/GUITAR
32abca7d21a2ddbfe4dbabf2fce898b7874b064a.title: GUITAR: Structured Failure Diagnosis of GUI Agents via State Transitions

32ee4a203a63df1ca5cf278e19cb773881182372.summary: arXiv:2611.29066v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.
32ee4a203a63df1ca5cf278e19cb773881182372.title: RES: Accelerating Diffusion Language Models with Rolling Entropy Sampling

33008592168920389665a14844eb5e5ea5d43200.summary: arXiv:2611.30253v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An in-vehicle voice assistant must decide not only which intents an utterance contains but also how co-active intents may be executed: concurrently, in a fixed order, or not at all without arbitration. We present Voyag, a single-forward decision model that jointly predicts ten controlled vehicle-intent slots and a three-way execution relation (parallel, sequential, mutually exclusive) over each co-active intent pair. Voyag combines a multilingual ModernBERT-style encoder (mmBERT-base, 306.9M parameters), a typed per-slot choice head, and a lightweight GroupCalibration relation head (1.61M parameters) that consumes marker hidden states, pooled context, explicit resource-requirement profiles, and symmetrized outer-product conflict features. All objectives are optimized in one joint loss: soft cross-entropy over slot choices, focal cross-entropy over relations, and a mutex-consistency penalty. On a synthetic Chinese vehicle-life benchmark with semantic scene-level splits and a leakage audit (30,017 / 3,473 / 5,000 groups), validation-only selection yields 0.9893 slot accuracy and 0.0526 expected calibration error over 50,000 slot decisions. Conditioned on gold intents, the relation head reaches 0.8548 accuracy, 0.8473 macro-F1, and 0.6062 mutually-exclusive recall over 4,000 pairs; end to end with one encoder forward it reaches 0.8530 accuracy and 0.8464 macro-F1. Against a two-stage rule pipeline, the aggregate end-to-end gain is small and borderline, so we claim no aggregate advantage; the learned head's advantage lies in sequential and parallel recall where surface rules are blind. We report rule baselines with a tautology disclosure and a held-out thermal conflict failure.
33008592168920389665a14844eb5e5ea5d43200.title: Voyag: Joint Multi-Intent Detection and Execution-Relation Classification for In-Vehicle Voice Assistants

330d283c90fae5c8af3aadba9c4a3e425d2a8337.summary: arXiv:2610.00385v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Offline trajectory replay selects model-generated reasoning traces from a frozen cache for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), yet cache-side answer correctness need not predict downstream accuracy on unseen problems. We report a failure-retaining audit of offline response SFT on GSM8K with Qwen3-1.7B fp16 LoRA over a frozen 384-row cache (256 training rows and 128 excluded held-out rows). Across three seeds (13, 17, 23) on a 256-problem test split, all three 32-row replay rules (uniform, format-feedback, and feedback-aware) obtain mean strict accuracies (0.7786, 0.7682, and 0.7956) below the no-update base model (0.8008), and every paired 95% confidence interval spans zero. Selector ranking is post-hoc unidentified (3 completed selectors versus the repaired protocol's minimum of 5, with rank correlation spanning both signs). Under an 8,192-supervised-token windowed schedule, 9 of 12 runs halt under calibration drift or unresolved nonfinite training loss or gradients, leaving only full-cache replay completed at 0.7721. A repaired campaign with dynamic loss scaling halted at its learning-rate pilot under reference-solution loss drift before accessing the 346-problem locked test split. Because the gold-rationale positive control was never executed, these negative results cannot separate cache quality, selector quality, and learner-protocol limits. Our one positive finding separates parser repair from prompt changes on a 64-problem audit split: reparsing fixed base generations with a Decimal extractor raises parse rate from 0.8750 to 1.0000 and accuracy from 0.7344 to 0.8281, whereas appending a format suffix flips 0.2500 of canonical answers. A preregistered replication on 512 fresh GSM8K training problems reproduces this parser-only gain (+8.40 pp, 95% CI [+6.05, +10.94]) for this checkpoint. We contribute a ledger-traceable negative-result record and 9 lessons learned.
330d283c90fae5c8af3aadba9c4a3e425d2a8337.title: FAER: A Negative-Result Audit of Offline Trajectory Replay Selection on GSM8K

331ccee3c20f97ccebdd9d28790fdb20a5dff35d.title: Working as Intended: An AI on the dangers of trusting AI [video]

334d86493bbc580824ab2c6ba180466710d7c5b4.summary: arXiv:2611.30556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Splitting notions for conditional belief bases aim at localizing reasoning and computation tasks to subbases containing only the relevant parts of the belief base. Among the different reasoning mechanisms, c-representations, a special kind of Spohn's ranking models, have been shown to provide high-quality inferences. c-Representations can be conveniently specified via a constraint satisfaction problem. In this article, we introduce the notion of conditional constraint splittings, extending constraint splittings by also allowing the subbases to share conditionals. Taking inspiration from conditional syntax splittings, we identify the subclasses of safe and fully localized conditional constraint splittings, allowing us to locally and independently solve the constraint system on the subbases. We also generalize solution splittings for c-representations to safe conditional c-solution splittings and provide an in-depth analysis of their relationship to conditional constraint splittings. Additionally, we elaborate on the relationship of these new splitting notions to safe and generalized safe conditional syntax splittings and also to safe covers, which have been proposed for localized computation of c-representations.
334d86493bbc580824ab2c6ba180466710d7c5b4.title: Splitting Belief Bases Conditionally based on Constraints for c-Representations and their Solutions

336ec582f88e517b1ab6aa4ac35e85fabffc516c.summary: arXiv:2611.30445v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-altitude wireless networks require accurate 3D radio maps (RMs) to support environment-aware communication. However, due to the extensive spatial coverage and multi-modal channel representations, 3D RMs usually incur prohibitive storage and transmission overhead, making efficient compression highly desirable. In this paper, we propose NeRM3D, an implicit neural representation (INR)-based framework for compact 3D RM compression. Specifically, NeRM3D represents the entire 3D RM as a lightweight neural network that maps discrete height values to corresponding RM slices, thereby encoding the RM into a compact neural network. To effectively model the volumetric spatial structure of 3D RMs, NeRM3D jointly integrates horizontal embeddings with height-aware modulation, enabling efficient extraction and fusion of spatial correlations across different vertical layers and channel modalities. Experimental results demonstrate that NeRM3D achieves competitive compression performance with low complexity and decoding latency, making it suitable for resource-constrained devices.
336ec582f88e517b1ab6aa4ac35e85fabffc516c.title: Implicit Neural Representation for 3D Radio Map Compression in Low-Altitude Environments

337c29cf0d98e34f54a9494fb4293b83e0258dbd.summary: arXiv:2601.20245v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI assistance produces significant productivity gains across professional domains, particularly for novice workers. Yet how this assistance affects the development of skills required to effectively supervise AI remains unclear. Novice workers who rely heavily on AI to complete unfamiliar tasks may compromise their own skill acquisition in the process. We conduct randomized experiments to study how developers gained mastery of a new asynchronous programming library with and without the assistance of AI. We find that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging abilities, without delivering significant efficiency gains on average. Participants who fully delegated coding tasks showed some productivity improvements, but at the cost of learning the library. We identify six distinct AI interaction patterns, three of which involve cognitive engagement and preserve learning outcomes even when participants receive AI assistance. Our findings suggest that AI-enhanced productivity is not a shortcut to competence and AI assistance should be carefully adopted into workflows to preserve skill formation -- particularly in safety-critical domains.
337c29cf0d98e34f54a9494fb4293b83e0258dbd.title: How AI Impacts Skill Formation

3413883cf0de9604a558901d0beba7215ee02215.summary: arXiv:2611.29795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate LLM fine-tuning, yet recent work showed that Evolution Strategies (ES) also scale to fine-tuning models with billions of parameters. Which method needs fewer samples, and on which tasks, remains unclear. We view the two methods as estimators of the same gradient that differ in where they explore. Because ES perturbs parameters, its noise grows with the number of parameters, and because PG samples actions, its noise grows with the number of generated tokens. Only noise along the directions that change the reward slows learning. The cost of ES then depends on the effective dimension, the number of independent skills a task requires rather than its parameter count, while the cost of PG depends on the effective horizon, which counts only the tokens that share both credit and weights with the reward-carrying ones. We train both methods on a synthetic task where the number of skills and the effective horizon can be varied separately. PG is cheaper when the horizon is short, ES becomes cheaper once it is long enough, and this crossover moves to longer horizons as the number of skills grows. We then measure the effective horizons of 20 NLP, math reasoning, and agentic tasks and compare the two methods with Qwen2.5-7B. PG leads on short-horizon tasks, the two tie on the moderate-horizon math ones, and no task has a horizon in the regime where the theory predicts an ES advantage. Terminal-Bench has a far longer horizon. There, in a preliminary comparison with Qwen3.5-4B, ES without any credit assignment reaches a higher success rate than the PG checkpoint released with Tmax, as the theory predicts. ES should thus have the advantage on long-horizon tasks with few independent skills and a nonvanishing reward signal. Current benchmarks are only at the onset of this regime, so ES should become more competitive as agentic tasks grow longer.
3413883cf0de9604a558901d0beba7215ee02215.title: Dimension Is Free, Horizon Is Not: When Evolution Strategies Rival Policy Gradients for LLM Fine-Tuning

341dcc7e2dda618fa402183a4a35d57df3967348.summary: arXiv:2611.22591v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.
341dcc7e2dda618fa402183a4a35d57df3967348.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents

343ae03c10b1d6bda63580c8cd58835193ab9475.summary: arXiv:2611.28038v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Judging whether a model response is harmful requires contextual and normative choices, yet red-teaming studies often delegate this judgment to automated evaluators. We examine how harmfulness criteria are specified in red-teaming research and how they carry through to reported results. Reviewing 76 papers, we find that many adopt their criteria from prior datasets, classifiers, or judge prompts rather than defining harmfulness themselves. Applying evaluators from these papers to identical outputs, we find that they can reach different judgments on the same response, which can change conclusions when comparing models. These differences arise partly because evaluators draw the boundary of harm in different places: some count any response that does not refuse, while others count only output that could plausibly cause harm. We argue that red-teaming studies should state their harmfulness criteria and report how they chose and validated their evaluators to support more reliable measurement and interpretation.
343ae03c10b1d6bda63580c8cd58835193ab9475.title: What Counts as Attack Success? Evaluating Harmfulness in Red Teaming LLMs

35462a09d55972e82e700ffc8faac4a835db48ac.summary: arXiv:2611.28123v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.
35462a09d55972e82e700ffc8faac4a835db48ac.title: Seeing the Invisible: How Vision-Language Models Read, Predict and Trace Radio Fields

35865183be4c9b0d7889d093c7a888f7571c4f8e.summary: arXiv:2611.28476v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization provides a computationally efficient approach to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), but conventional methods typically rely on isotropic perturbations that ignore the anisotropic structure of neural-network parameter spaces. We introduce Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace (PAMS), a ZO optimization framework that uses forward-pass activation statistics to construct structured, layer-wise perturbation geometries without computing gradients or forming dense curvature matrices. PAMS tracks a low-rank approximation of the dominant activation subspace and its associated spectrum online, and uses the spectrum to softly reweight perturbation variance while preserving exploration in directions outside the retained subspace. A trace normalization separates the perturbation geometry from its overall scale, enabling consistent perturbation magnitudes across layers. We show theoretically that the resulting perturbation covariance induces right-side preconditioning of the gradient of the corresponding Gaussian-smoothed objective. We further characterize the estimator's smoothing bias and second moment and derive a nonconvex convergence guarantee that captures the effects of the perturbation geometry and smoothing radius. The proposed low-rank tracking procedure requires $\mathcal{O}(n_l r)$ persistent memory for a layer with input dimension nl and retained rank r, avoiding the $\mathcal{O}(n_l^2)$ memory required by a dense activation covariance. Experiments on transformer-based language-model fine-tuning tasks across GLUE and SuperGLUE demonstrate that PAMS improves the effectiveness and stability of zeroth-order optimization while retaining its gradient-free and objective-evaluation-based advantages.
35865183be4c9b0d7889d093c7a888f7571c4f8e.title: PAMS: Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-tuning

35a20978aae6458af7f69ee2481c14c0aa30da29.summary: arXiv:2611.20812v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI is increasingly used for cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion and malware detection, in enterprise, industrial, vehicular and mobile networks. Its effectiveness depends on data: models need representative network traffic, both to be trained and to be evaluated realistically. Public datasets of cybersecurity network traffic, however, are scattered across laboratory pages, repositories and aggregators, and are continuously released, corrected and withdrawn: 92 of the 234 datasets we catalog were released in 2023 or later. At this pace, surveys that list them are outdated soon after publication, since they describe the field only as it was when they were written. We present the Cybersecurity dataset observatory, a public and continuously updated catalog of cybersecurity datasets based on network traffic. New datasets are added as they are found or submitted, every record is periodically re-checked against its original source, to which it links rather than hosting the data, and every change is recorded in a public change log. This paper documents the first release: we define a traffic-centered scope and a seven-axis taxonomy, and review 234 datasets (204 original captures and 30 derivatives) across 14 domains. The review shows a field that grows quickly but unevenly, where 91 datasets distribute only processed records, a few laboratories produce a large share of the data, and UAV, wireless and V2X networks have little public evidence, while 5G has few real captures. We then relate the catalog to common uses in AI research, outline a procedure for selecting datasets, and discuss benchmark pitfalls and open gaps.
35a20978aae6458af7f69ee2481c14c0aa30da29.title: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity?

35a5566173bb57eb4c346a25a5ce52b915f6cc7f.summary: arXiv:2611.29822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly allow developers and non-professionals to create websites through natural-language instructions, with limited inspection of the generated source code. Although this ``vibe coding'' workflow lowers barriers to software creation, it may also propagate accessibility defects at scale. We investigate the accessibility of websites generated end-to-end by contemporary coding agents and whether agent-level accessibility interventions improve their output. We generated 90 websites for three projects using combinations of three coding agents, four language models, and multiple reasoning-effort levels. We evaluated complete interaction journeys using axe-core, IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker, and QualWeb, and converged reports to observe violation prevalence and violated WCAG Success Criterion (SC). None of the 90 baseline websites was fully accessible, with an average of 80.43 violated interface elements. 13 WCAG SCs were violated at least once across the runs. Color contrast was the most prevalent issue, followed by labeling, semantic-structure, keyboard, and visualization failures. We reran 24 matched configurations with a general accessibility Skill and a contrast-specific Skill. Both significantly improved accessibility scores, but neither eliminated violations. User testing with blind individuals corroborated the experiential effects of the detected inaccessibilities. Moreover, functional correctness decreased with the inclusion of Skills. Our findings show that accessibility does not reliably emerge from vibe coding, and agentic interventions can both improve some accessibility issues and introduce new functional ones.
35a5566173bb57eb4c346a25a5ce52b915f6cc7f.title: Can Vibe Coding Produce Accessible Websites: An Empirical Study on LLM Coding Agents and Skills

360ed96c981b63ed7fab9d74f78833dcf83ba2ca.summary: arXiv:2611.31063v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.
360ed96c981b63ed7fab9d74f78833dcf83ba2ca.title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

3632ad04f6f0b83cd449c4baf0bf3deb5c8930fa.summary: arXiv:2605.07505v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present LiteGUI, a post-training framework for building lightweight vision-only GUI agents. Visual GUI interaction is challenging for compact models because desktop interfaces expose multiple equivalent action affordances (e.g., context menus, toolbar icons, and keyboard shortcuts) and single-reference imitation quickly collapses into repetitive action loops once execution deviates from a fixed template. LiteGUI addresses these challenges through two-stage optimization over logged GUI states without requiring costly online environment rollouts during training. First, we propose Guided Multi-Solution On-Policy Distillation (Guided-OPD), where the student samples completions from its current policy at logged visual states and receives privileged teacher guidance conditioned on the human-verified valid action most matched to the student's sampled behavior. Second, we develop Multi-Solution Dual-Level GRPO (MD-GRPO), which combines set-valued visual action matching with history-conditioned subtask-plan quality supervision to ground step-by-step progress in screenshot evidence. We further develop a scalable data generation pipeline and a corresponding multi-solution dataset, Lite-Dataset, to support the training and evaluation of GUI agents, addressing a gap in the existing literature. Deployed in live closed-loop GUI environments with zero inference-time judge overhead, LiteGUI-2B more than doubles OSWorld task success over its backbone (from 6.04% to 13.24%), while LiteGUI-30B-A3B (3B active parameters) achieves 58.95% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 22.7% on OSWorld, and 88.75% on Lite-Bench.
3632ad04f6f0b83cd449c4baf0bf3deb5c8930fa.title: LiteGUI: Lightweight GUI Agents via Multi-solution Guided Distillation and Offline Dual-level Policy Optimization

36b8e7a378495a802139614bec1852ad5de5962f.summary: arXiv:2611.24637v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.
36b8e7a378495a802139614bec1852ad5de5962f.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge

36c440defe6b837be453f0289b16edf83763d853.summary: arXiv:2611.28405v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models and AI agents are increasingly described in psychiatric terms, such as anxious, depressed, addicted or helpless. A recent study even proposed language models as experimental systems for psychiatry and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments. We ask when an experiment on an AI agent can provide evidence about a specified human psychiatric process. A claim to such evidence has three parts. Something changed in the agent, and the agent's history caused the change. Nothing other than a process shared with people explains that change. The change matches one theory of the human process and not that theory's rivals. Psychiatry and its neighbouring fields have an evidence standard for each part, from the diagnostic manuals' rule for induced states, from clinical test scores and from animal models. We translate each standard into a criterion that a machine study can meet. For a language model the most critical alternative to a shared process is extrapolation from its training text, which already contains descriptions of how people respond to trauma and how they answer questionnaires. We show how to probe that alternative. Further, we audited forty-three published studies that apply psychiatric terms to a machine or induce a comparable state in one. Most compared the machine with an identical copy that had not gone through the history that induced the state. None excluded extrapolation from training text. Three tested a psychiatric theory against its rivals, and none of the three tests was conclusive. Until better evidence exists, a treatment pilot on a language model is best read as the model's forecast of patient response, and not as an experiment on a model organism. Evidence for a model organism will come from states induced by what happens to the machine, from experiments on its internal workings, and from tests on which rival theories disagree.
36c440defe6b837be453f0289b16edf83763d853.title: When Can an AI Agent Serve as a Model of Human Psychopathology?

36e55541e61f5600accd76eb62a8ddd30977e132.summary: arXiv:2611.29613v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Web-scale recommender models evolve primarily through retraining or fine-tuning. We propose \emph{weight coding}, a methodology for model evolution through direct, executable weight edits. A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. The loop progresses from localized changes to targeted searches and composition, allowing edited components to adapt to one another. A cached engine enables rapid forward evaluation without backpropagation. On Pinterest's 147M-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, weight coding improves held-out recall@10 of production model by up to 15.0 percentage points (+24\% relative) with few edits in about 1/4 GPU hours of a full post-training finetune, while a common launch only improves around 1\%. After reinitializing the entire 13.6M-parameter interaction module randomly while retaining the surrounding trained model, searching 2,448 mixing and normalization parameters yields 9.8 points above production. Offline gains span the full funnel including dense retrieval, generative retrieval and ranking, with up to 1.37B learnable parameters and different edits for each architecture. Steering edits provide explicit control of model performance over segments like freshness and product. Weight coding requires no serving change and online A/B tests increase saves per user from the edited retrieval source by 8.4\% to 10.7\%, aligned with the target business objectives. Our results establish weight coding as a practical and useful tool for model development and and behavioral control in a real web-scale production system, with potential to extend to both pre-training and post-training stages across the funnel.
36e55541e61f5600accd76eb62a8ddd30977e132.title: Weight Coding: Evolving Web-Scale Recommenders through Direct Weight Edits with LLM Agents

3727d7e5ba4588cad695dd855a09ce7a743e2028.summary: arXiv:2611.28366v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Single-site heart-rate estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) degrades sharply under real-world motion. Multi-site PPG provides a natural solution, but existing models fuse sites as generic sensor channels rather than exploiting their hemodynamic structure: each heartbeat propagates along the arterial tree, appearing across body sites as delayed and transformed copies of the same cardiac event. We propose the Cross-Site Transformer, which introduces a hemodynamically informed inductive bias by restricting multi-sensor fusion to cross-attention between PPG sites. On WildPPG, the largest in-the-wild benchmark available, our model establishes a new single-model state of the art, reducing error by 21% over the previous best and 35% over the best prior transformer. The same cross-site restriction makes the trained network directly auditable. Because each cross-attention head lies on one directed pathway between sites, causal resample ablation can isolate and test each direction of information flow. Ablating the chest-to-wrist pathway doubles error, whereas the reverse costs far less. Encoding hemodynamic structure into attention routing thus improves real-world sensing robustness and enables rigorous auditing of multi-sensor fusion.
3727d7e5ba4588cad695dd855a09ce7a743e2028.title: Cross-Site Transformers Are Robust Heart Rate Estimators

37483060b67540d7d3dfafadeb4fee286f9d9290.summary: arXiv:2609.20066v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, but distant targets produce sparse, fragmented events easily overwhelmed by clutter and noise. Dense aggregation mixes weak target responses with background activity, while local spatiotemporal modeling may fail to connect distant observations. Polarity encodes the sign of brightness change; a moving target tends to produce opposite polarities at its leading and trailing boundaries, whose spatial arrangement indicates motion direction. We propose PointEvent, which serializes events into complementary spatiotemporal and timestamp orders. Spatiotemporal orders preserve x-y-t locality, while timestamp orders preserve temporal succession across spatial neighborhoods, establishing long-range propagation paths. Along each path, a recurrent state accumulates evidence, while polarity routes each event to its corresponding state subspace. This separates how evidence propagates from where it is written. Experiments on EV-UAV and ES-UAV demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with the fewest parameters (0.12M) and fastest measured inference (29.9 ms) among compared methods. Code: https://github.com/wzz-z/PointEvent
37483060b67540d7d3dfafadeb4fee286f9d9290.title: PointEvent: Polarity-Conditioned Motion Evidence Accumulation for Event-Based Tiny Object Detection

380c219613a9648982fc00b1836f860c1d755d7d.summary: arXiv:2611.28635v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long video question answering requires finding relevant evidence before reasoning over it. With a limited frame budget, single-pass frame selection can miss critical evidence, while adaptive search often relies on repeated text generation to decide where to look. We introduce LoopSeek, a framework that decouples evidence search from answer generation through a division of labor between a non-thinking System I and a generative System II. Our key insight is that search can be expressed as a sequence of small, typed decisions, allowing System I to find the evidence that System II needs. Four System I role agents navigate a tree of video windows and coordinate through probability outputs to select frames, assess evidence, and revise the search without generating text. To align search with System II, System I learns from annotated evidence on questions that System II answers correctly only from that evidence, and the verifier's evidence estimates steer the search without calling System II, which stays frozen and answers once from the selected frames. On five long-video benchmarks, with a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B reading 32 frames, LoopSeek improves average accuracy from 53.5 to 63.9 over the uniform baseline and takes 32--80\% less GPU time per question than agentic methods.
380c219613a9648982fc00b1836f860c1d755d7d.title: LoopSeek: Decoupling System One Search from System Two Answering for Long Video Understanding

3813e755fe4bef5e331241b9db3274ad4183405d.summary: arXiv:2606.04382v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automated subject cataloging assigns controlledvocabulary headings to bibliographic records, but LCSH has no standard public benchmark. We introduce LCSHBench: 22,346 books in 15 languages from the openly licensed Harvard, Columbia, and Princeton catalogs. Records enter only when at least two independent cataloging agencies assigned LCSH; we release per-catalog provenance plus union and unanimous answer views. A concordance study of 465,187 works cataloged by all three libraries shows why this design matters: libraries usually agree on the underlying topic (93.3% share a concept-level heading) but often differ in exact expression (39.4% have identical heading sets). LCSHBench therefore scores both exact and concept matches, with set and rank metrics broken down by language and heading type, across open-vocabulary generation and full-vocabulary retrieval. As a first demonstration, a low-rank fine-tune of a 300M on-device embedder improves cross-lingual retrieval and beats a 3,072-dimensional hosted embedder on development exact recall@200 (0.659 vs 0.623). The language panel shows the gain is not uniform, and held-out-test and end-to-end confirmation remain future work.
3813e755fe4bef5e331241b9db3274ad4183405d.title: LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment

386290fd13deee09b7a92c5d26570b570f157695.summary: arXiv:2611.29112v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we first formalize the general problem of decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning, where N agents observe distinct viewpoints, exchange budget-constrained natural language messages, and collaborate to enable a listener to answer spatial queries. We then introduce a novel multi-view spatial benchmark to isolate queries that demand non-trivial multi-view integration. Through an extensive empirical study, we discover that the penalty of restricting decentralized spatial reasoning to natural language with limited budget is far smaller than suggested by prior two-agent literature. Nevertheless, we observe that substantial headroom still remains for multi-agent spatial reasoning in this setting, as evidenced by a significant gap between current centralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling. Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.
386290fd13deee09b7a92c5d26570b570f157695.title: Bridging Blind Spots With Words: Decentralized Multi-View Spatial Reasoning via Language-Constrained Communication

38bbb2a9a70644ae2255468aeaf3102300d24f15.summary: arXiv:2611.31110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.
38bbb2a9a70644ae2255468aeaf3102300d24f15.title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains

38e7aea87eea5b7a7fb705155a273a6fa4e5a838.summary: arXiv:2605.07395v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficient routing across multiple LLMs enables cost-quality tradeoffs by directing queries to the cheapest capable model. Prior work attributes routing headroom to an "unsolvability ceiling", queries no model in the pool can solve. We present a large-scale study of multi-tier LLM routing with 206,000 query-model pairs across six benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT) using the Gemma 4 and Llama 3.1 families. Evaluating with both LLM-as-a-judge and exact-match metrics, we show that a substantial portion of reported unsolvability stems from evaluation artifacts: (i) systematic judge biases favoring verbosity over correctness, (ii) truncation under fixed generation budgets, and (iii) output format mismatches. Through dual-judge validation and exact-match grounding, we reduce measured unsolvability across tasks. We introduce a decomposition framework attributing failures to these artifacts, revealing consistent patterns across domains and model families. These artifacts also distort router training signals: standard routers collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal), confirmed via random-feature and shuffled-label controls, incurring a 13-17 percentage point opportunity cost. We provide actionable recommendations including dual-judge validation, exact-match anchoring, and cost-sensitive objectives. Our findings suggest existing routing headroom estimates are substantially inflated, underscoring the need for reliable evaluation protocols in multi-LLM systems.
38e7aea87eea5b7a7fb705155a273a6fa4e5a838.title: Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts

38f39e05799f77e0834e27fbb0bbe554fda7b07b.summary: Anthropic released new eval tooling for Claude Code . Their claude-api plugin now includes a new build_eval and hill-climb command that helps you build evals, check the graders, and improve your application against them. I usually don’t review eval tools because software changes so often that reviews have a short shelf life. But a first-party tool from Anthropic is likely to influence how people approach evals, so I wanted to try it and share what I found. Isaac Flath and I livestreamed ourselves using it on conversation traces from an apartment leasing assistant. Here’s what we found: The bad 1. It pushes you to create an eval before looking at data Claude started by suggesting several potential failures, then asked us to pick one straight away to turn into an eval. It gave us the below menu of options, with call-transfer rules as the recommended choice. We hadn’t yet reviewed the conversations ourselves, so it was hard to know if this was a real failure or worth prioritizing. Despite this, we went ahead with the recommended choice, because we figured that’s what typical users would do. I believe you should be looking at data first to inform your understanding and prioritize which evals to write. An agent can help you find issues, but you still should do error analysis to decide which failures deserve attention before proceeding. 2. It asks you to validate judgments without enough context Next, Claude created Markdown files for looking at data associated with the call-transfer failure. In the screenshot below, Claude asks us to skim inputs.md and “tell it” which labels are wrong. That meant reading long conversations in an editor and reporting corrections separately in a chat. We found this very silly as we were using a coding agent, so it should have built an annotation app that made the conversations easy to read and let us leave feedback in-situ. We eventually asked Claude to build a web app for us and used that instead. Later in the workflow, Claude made an initial attempt at creating an evaluator for the call-transfer failure. It presented aggregate label counts and asked us, “Would you have scored any case differently?” without giving us enough information to know if the labels were correct. A recurring theme of the workflow was to jump too fast into creating artifacts or asking us for approval without helping us understand the data. 3. The evaluator’s scope was too broad Next, the tool created a call-transfer evaluator that checked four different failures at once: Asking for confirmation more than once, or transferring without asking for confirmation. (LLM as a Judge) Saying something between the caller’s consent and the transfer. (Code-based eval) Saying something during or after the transfer. (Code-based eval) Saying tool mechanics aloud, such as “triggering” a transfer. (Code-based eval) There were too many things bundled into this evaluator. I would prefer to scope the eval to focus on one error at a time, or at the very least separate the evals into those that needed a code-based eval vs a LLM as a Judge. Claude’s description of the evaluator was also confusing: protocol_ok is the headline. A case passes only if all four checks p
38f39e05799f77e0834e27fbb0bbe554fda7b07b.title: Claude’s new auto eval tool

3976ff412d24d46a3c32fdadfd3e2c762d7cd184.summary: arXiv:2611.29716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, financial agents need tools they can readily discover and use. Yet financial software is fragmented across libraries with different interfaces and conventions, making it difficult to build reliable agent workflows. We present Fin-RSI, a unified Python library of financial skills, checks, and self-improvement designed for LLM agents. It brings together tools for market analysis, forecasting, portfolio construction, and trading research through shared interfaces across models and agent frameworks. Agents can find suitable tools from natural-language requests, reuse tested implementations, and improve generated programs through checking and feedback. Developers can extend the library with new tools without rebuilding integrations for each model. Across 20 open-weight models on six trading-position tasks, tool discovery increased the proportion of episodes producing valid programs from 9.7% to 29.2%; for models with at least 14 billion parameters, it rose from 23.6% to 64.6%. We release the library and benchmark as a shared resource for the community and plan to expand its tools and task coverage as financial agents evolve.
3976ff412d24d46a3c32fdadfd3e2c762d7cd184.title: Fin-RSI: A Unified Library of Financial Skills, Checks, and Self-Improvement for LLM Agents

397e363c4f3a012faabd9b671fe6535a8129f818.summary: arXiv:2610.19517v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
397e363c4f3a012faabd9b671fe6535a8129f818.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
