4a77e7d5e2b1852935ea9c2e77fdaad46f9ad79f.summary: arXiv:2611.26316v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.
4a77e7d5e2b1852935ea9c2e77fdaad46f9ad79f.title: C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology

4a7944a6b20a53a7738df5435073f916d239f136.summary: arXiv:2611.28202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.
4a7944a6b20a53a7738df5435073f916d239f136.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay

4a7a001691f20578741b0c2d389b86044c413b74.summary: arXiv:2606.04987v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-party dialogue is a critical setting for studying collaborative reasoning and decision-making, yet existing datasets rarely focus on structured, reasoning-intensive tasks. We introduce DeliChess, a dataset of group deliberation dialogues in which participants collaboratively solve multiple-choice chess puzzles. Participants first answer independently, then engage in multi-party deliberation and revise their individual answers. The dataset comprises 107 sessions containing 321 puzzle discussions across 24 unique positions, with full transcripts, pre- and post-deliberation choices, and utterance-level annotations of communicative function, epistemic stance, and usefulness in supporting deliberation. Our analyses show that greater diversity in initial solution quality is associated with larger gains, while answer trajectories reveal how deliberation can recover, discover, or lose strong answers. Cases in which groups surpass every independent answer are associated with sustained reasoning and epistemic openness. We further propose a diagnostic action-selection task: the tested LLMs show limited exact agreement with human-attested helpful actions, while ranked predictions reveal partial alignment. Overall, our dataset provides a testbed for modelling group reasoning, dialogue dynamics, and conditions for effective deliberation.
4a7a001691f20578741b0c2d389b86044c413b74.title: DeliChess: A Multi-party Dialogue Dataset for Deliberation in Chess Puzzle Solving

4a93c5c414343571bfe2f57912e3e001b1732f64.summary: arXiv:2611.29982v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue hardware signals, such as power draw, have been proposed as a potential information channel for compute verification. Such signals can be measured externally, without the operator's cooperation. We show that the supply current drawn by a GPU can be used to verify the work declared by the GPU operator, without requiring examples of prohibited workloads or evasion strategies. We record 23.4 h of GPU current with a Rogowski coil under idle, training and inference workloads. We consider five evasion strategies an operator might use to disguise prohibited training. We show that a one-class model fitted to the current draw of permitted, declared work (idle and inference) flags at least 99.9% of windows of prohibited training, including training hidden by the five evasion strategies. As a continuous monitor across successive windows, it detects all 188 episodes of prohibited training hidden by time-sharing with declared inference, with a median delay of 3.0 s, and raises one alarm in 8.8 h of declared work. Incomplete or corrupt recordings of the declared work can undermine verification. An incomplete recording fails loudly; with idle missing, the monitor is in alarm for 99.97% of declared idle. A corrupt recording can fail silently; if the operator runs training during the recording, the monitor can miss hidden training while raising no alarm on declared work. These results suggest that operator declarations together with external analogue sensing might offer a practical route to compute verification.
4a93c5c414343571bfe2f57912e3e001b1732f64.title: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current

4b418d5b0b1cd9afe1643f47c19f9791fbe2f1c0.summary: arXiv:2609.19759v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When should a task be delegated to subagents? We answer this at the granularity of individual trajectories. Modeling a trajectory as a dependency graph, we identify bridge edges, whose removal separates the trajectory into independent components, and show that the agent orchestration pattern should match this bridge-edge structure. Our experiments on long-horizon benchmarks indicate that subagents tend to benefit sparse bridge-edge structures, whereas tightly coupled trajectories are often better handled by a single agent. We instantiate this principle as SAIGE, a lightweight mechanism that spawns subagents only at predicted bridge edges and resolves their connections lazily, achieving a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance where the structure admits decomposition. We further observe that scaling the agent pool or recursion depth does not reliably help, in line with the view that orchestration should follow the bridge-edge pattern.
4b418d5b0b1cd9afe1643f47c19f9791fbe2f1c0.title: When to Use Subagents

4b5dd336573b04c7c37d4ca8baeceea555730d9e.summary: arXiv:2605.22973v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many novel unsupervised feature selection methods are proposed each year, yet their empirical evaluation is limited to supervised and unsupervised evaluation metrics computed on selected datasets, along with comparisons to existing methods. However, in the absence of an established evaluation baseline, it is difficult to determine the value added to the existing literature by each of these methods, and how effective their underlying approaches are. In this evaluation study, we are using random feature selection as a baseline for evaluating unsupervised feature selection methods. While a random selection of features might seem to be a rather weak baseline, we show in this evaluation study that many of the state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised feature selection are outperformed by random feature selection in both performance and efficiency. Accordingly, we emphasize the strict requirement of considering random feature selection as a baseline in the development process of novel unsupervised feature selection methods, and we encourage the community to develop better evaluation measures for feature selection. Both would help to ensure consistent improvement and realistic assessment.
4b5dd336573b04c7c37d4ca8baeceea555730d9e.title: Worse than Random: The Importance of a Baseline for Unsupervised Feature Selection -- Extended Version

4b693a449bc4f9c628c11908f26b6cc9a6bca5e3.summary: arXiv:2611.29381v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diagonal Green functions of a periodic Jacobi operator on a universal covering tree satisfy the scalar Gaussian belief propagation covariance equations on the finite connected loopless base multigraph. At cycle rank at least two, the Green functions continue to simple antibound poles at both Perron values for arbitrary real potentials and nonzero real weights. This proves the conjecture of Christiansen, Simon and Zinchenko. For positive weights the pole result includes self-loops. On loopless graphs the lower pole is the walk-summability threshold. Each energy strictly between it and the spectral bottom has at least two fixed points with positive definite local beliefs. On a connected simple graph, some coefficients yield a compact component of positive solutions exactly when the graph contains two vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of cycle rank at least two. The covariance curve is generically irreducible, with one sheet per edge subset with no vertex of degree one. For cycle rank at least two and generic real coefficients, the diagonal Green functions, infinite half-tree $m$-functions and the density-of-states Stieltjes transform all have this degree, answering a question of Avni, Breuer and Simon. Then all eigenvalues of the signed Jacobi matrices are antibound poles. Signed principal submatrices classify finite points with nonzero residue of $(\sum_i V_i) dz$, where $V_i$ are the vertex variances. We give a genus formula. Near zero potentials and unit weights on $K_4$, independently varying the coefficients leaves the cover spectrum an interval. This refutes Avni, Breuer and Simon's conjecture on the density of parameters with all gaps open. In block models, generic irreducibility and a uniqueness criterion extend, and at uniform dimension $p$ the degree can exceed $L^p$ for scalar degree $L$. Part of the scalar theory is formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
4b693a449bc4f9c628c11908f26b6cc9a6bca5e3.title: Gaussian Belief Propagation and Periodic Jacobi Matrices on Trees: Spectral Curve, Antibound Poles, and Fixed Points

4b6dbdd12da73c29e5a576fa5b3f5ea18a7d141d.summary: arXiv:2605.05703v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optimizing the communication structure of large language model based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) has been shown to improve downstream performance and reduce token usage. Existing methods typically train on randomly sampled tasks. We show that this optimization is sensitive to the choice of training tasks: downstream accuracy varies widely across random task sets, and adding more random tasks does not consistently improve it. To actively identify the most valuable tasks from a pool of task-answer pairs, we propose an ensemble-based information-theoretic task selection framework. It estimates task informativeness by how much a candidate task changes the distribution over graph parameters, using ensemble Kalman inversion as an efficient and derivative-free approximation of the Bayesian update. The resulting estimator is especially suitable for black-box and noisy multi-agent systems and remains effective with ensembles much smaller than the parameter dimension. To further reduce the number of tasks whose informativeness must be evaluated, we introduce representative pre-selection and surrogate modeling. We validate the framework in benign and adversarial settings and across multiple task formats. It outperforms random training, demonstrating more effective task selection and greater overall cost efficiency.
4b6dbdd12da73c29e5a576fa5b3f5ea18a7d141d.title: Active Learning for Communication Structure Optimization in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

4bbeb4ada01e1126e84a8feadc36c2f016273f4f.summary: arXiv:2611.28819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Formalizing mathematics in Lean is never a word-for-word translation of a paper: a Lean formalization changes definitions, strengthens hypotheses, splits arguments, and adds lemmas the paper never mentions. It stands to reason that a model that is good at autoformalization must be a good predictor of how a natural language source must differ from its faithful Lean formalization. With that in mind, we collect 4{,}076 audited examples of such changes from 832 Lean projects that formalize research-level mathematics, and use them to ask a practical question: how well can a model \emph{write} Lean inside a real research-level project that may contain tens of thousands of lines of code, and does training on discrepancies between natural language sources and their faithful Lean formalizations help? Our training set consists of 3{,}431 tasks from 141 repositories, and the test set consists of 645 tasks from the remaining 27 repositories. Training on in-project Lean nearly doubles complete proofs ($11\% \to 20\%$) and raises the share of statements in gold agreement with the project's own formalization by nearly a third ($30\%$ to $39\%$). The gain comes from the pairs themselves: an adapter trained only to predict how the Lean will differ, or a model told the difference in advance, barely helps. Training on where formalizations depart from their sources is thus an effective way of improving semantic equivalence in research-level formalization.
4bbeb4ada01e1126e84a8feadc36c2f016273f4f.title: Improving semantic equivalence in research-level math formalization

4bdb6d39f683fd8715294b62ab9da2482b8fe5e8.summary: # Release v5.24.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is a smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small, added in v5.23.0. It has 24 decoder layers instead of 48, and compensates with a looping mechanism in which layers 6 to 17 run three times. A learned message-passing mechanism mixes the residuals of the previous pass into the attention and mixture-of-experts inputs of each loop layer. The decoder has a hidden size of 2304 and routes each token to 8 of 128 experts. The image encoder, tokenizer and processor are the same as Inkling 2 Small's. A research checkpoint ([TML-d24-varloop-research](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research)) has the same architecture but supports a variable number of loop passes. Fewer passes are faster, and more passes improve quality. Both checkpoints contain NVFP4 and MXFP8 quantized layers, which are dequantized at load time. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/inkling2_loop) | [Blog Post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) | [HF Blog Post](https://huggingface.co/blog/inkling2mini) * Add Inkling2 Mini (#51050) by @guarin ### Apertus 1.5 Apertus 1.5 is a multimodal model from the Swiss AI Initiative that accepts text, images and audio and generates text. It extends the Apertus language model with the EMU3.5 vision tokenizer for images and WavTokenizer for audio. The EMU3.5 tokenizer is an image-only VQGAN with the same encoder as Chameleon's, and it assigns codes by the largest inner product with the codebook. The media tokenizers turn images and audio into discrete tokens, which the language backbone processes alongside text in a shared input vocabulary. The output vocabulary contains only text tokens, so image and audio generation are not supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/apertus1p5) * Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft ### WavTokenizer WavTokenizer encodes 24 kHz mono audio into discrete tokens using a single codebook, at 40 or 75 tokens per second depending on the checkpoint, and reconstructs audio from those tokens. `WavTokenizerModel` encodes and decodes, and `WavTokenizerEncoderModel` only encodes. Speech, music/audio and unified checkpoints are available. The 40-token-per-second variant is the audio tokenizer of Apertus 1.5. Training the codec is not supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/wavtokenizer) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2408.16532) * Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft ### Dory Dory is a looped (latent-recurrent) language model from NVIDIA. It uses a normalized-GPT architecture with interleaved sliding-window and full attention layers. A shared block of layers is applied repeatedly, so Dory can spend more compute per token. The loop count can be changed at inference time on the same checkpoint to trade speed against quality. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/dory) | [Paper (nG
4bdb6d39f683fd8715294b62ab9da2482b8fe5e8.title: Release v5.24.0

4bf853a3aa26b5993eae110c4a8976e8f0085243.summary: arXiv:2611.31027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.

4c6bda70881340ba9178b396451559cf75f731c0.summary: arXiv:2611.28660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.
4c6bda70881340ba9178b396451559cf75f731c0.title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus

4cb19c63fc1a8dfc18233a9c6ad0da4fa5bb8217.summary: arXiv:2611.28586v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biomedical question answering often requires multi-step reasoning under limited inference budgets. While test-time search methods such as Tree-of-Thought can improve reasoning performance, directly searching over free-form language is computationally expensive and highly redundant, as many reasoning trajectories contain semantically equivalent intermediate steps expressed in different surface forms. We introduce MedCoast, an offline-to-online reasoning framework that converts sampled chain-of-thought trajectories into a compact space for structured process supervision. Offline, we recursively cluster semantically similar reasoning steps under shared prefixes to construct an abstract reasoning tree that captures recurring clinical reasoning patterns. We then derive node-level supervision from progress toward correct solutions, and train a lightweight process reward model (PRM) to evaluate partial reasoning states. At inference time, the learned critic guides test-time exploration by prioritizing promising reasoning prefixes. Across seven biomedical QA benchmarks, MedCoast often improves over self-consistency under fixed inference budgets, with gains of up to 15 points. Despite using a reward model more than 50 times smaller, MedCoast achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art reward models in several settings, highlighting its potential for resource-constrained biomedical reasoning.
4cb19c63fc1a8dfc18233a9c6ad0da4fa5bb8217.title: MedCoast: Semantic Abstraction of Reasoning Trajectories for Test-Time Biomedical Question Answering

4ccdd19da1ca239b7431cefbd9f14a6261a6b5fa.summary: arXiv:2611.28686v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale redistributable symbolic pop-melody data remain scarce due to copyright restrictions, creating a bottleneck for both practical deployment and reproducible research in music generation. We present PopMelodyGen, a copyright-aware platform for controllable pop-melody generation that combines rule-based synthesis with neural generation. Our approach first uses an expert synthesizer to produce large-scale labeled synthetic melodies from explicit musical knowledge and templates, providing scalable pretraining data with auditable provenance. A neural model is then pretrained on this corpus and adapted with a small licensed real-pop corpus to improve melodic naturalness while preserving controllability. The platform supports interactive melody creation with accompaniment playback and export for creators, as well as batch construction of annotated symbolic datasets for researchers. PopMelodyGen demonstrates a practical training and deployment paradigm for creative AI when large-scale reusable real-world data are limited.
4ccdd19da1ca239b7431cefbd9f14a6261a6b5fa.title: PopMelodyGen: A Copyright-Aware Platform for Controllable Pop-Melody Generation

4ce612ee14691da9a9ba4e17220e6582fcf56822.summary: # Inkling Fine-tuning You can now fine-tune Inkling 2 Mini 1.8 to 3.1x faster and use 50% less VRAM in Unsloth with LoRA or QLoRA, then export it to GGUF or a merged 16-bit model. It trains on Kaggle's free 2x T4 and now supports tensor, pipeline and context parallel across GPUs. Also new: faster `adamw_8bit` steps, faster Z-Image LoRA training on T4 and fixes for thinking models in chat. ## Highlights - **Fine-tune Inkling 2 Mini 3x faster + 50% less VRAM** in Unsloth Desktop. [Guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/inkling-2-mini/finetuning-inkling-2-mini) - **Faster Inkling 2 Mini inference** Fixed incorrect max context length (2-3x faster inference) - **Faster `adamw_8bit`** up to 12% less time per step on small batches - **Z-Image LoRA training on T4** 1.7x faster per step - **`unsloth eval` on chat fine-tunes** now scores your own datasets in the model's chat format ## Inkling 2 training - Train Inkling 2 Mini with LoRA or QLoRA, including the vision layers. It fits on Kaggle's 2x T4 at about 26 s per step, but not on a single 15 GB T4. - Inkling 2 Small is supported too but needs about 290 GB of GPU memory in 4-bit. - `save_pretrained_merged` with `merged_16bit` and `save_pretrained_gguf` now work for Inkling 2. `merged_4bit` is still not supported. - A fine-tuned Inkling 2 Mini exports to a 17.5 GB `q4_k_m` GGUF that runs in llama.cpp. The export needs about 150 GB of free disk, so use a Colab A100 instead of Kaggle. - On NVIDIA Ampere or newer GPUs, Inkling 2 training uses FlexAttention, about 15% faster per step on L4. ## Training - `optim = "adamw_8bit"` now updates each parameter group in one step, up to 12% less time per step on L4 with small batches. - GRPO rollouts with a 16-bit LoRA decode about 20% faster per token on L4. - Native FSDP2 full fine-tuning takes 17 to 21% less time per step on 2x T4. - AsyncGRPO tree packing now also covers Mamba2 models such as Nemotron-H and Granite-4.0-H, and LFM2, with newer TRL. - Left-padded training batches no longer let pad positions see future tokens. - `unsloth eval` on a chat fine-tune with your own .jsonl, .json or .csv dataset no longer scores near 0. - After `add_new_tokens` on a tied-embedding model, merged and GGUF exports no longer drop the trained `lm_head`. - Phi-3 and Phi-3.5 training text now ends with the EOS token again. - Chat datasets with custom keys such as `speaker` and `text` no longer get role and content swapped. ## Images + video - Z-Image LoRA training on T4 is 1.7x faster per step. - On 24 GB GPUs, MiniMax-H3-Image now denoises the images of a multi-image request together instead of one by one. - MiniMax-H3 video re-renders with the same reference clip or keyframe skip re-encoding it. - FLUX.3 Klein base has an opt-in Fast CFG switch, about 10% faster renders with a small image change. - On AMD Strix Halo, FLUX.2 klein 4B LoRA training takes about 11% less time per step. - Krea 2 no longer gets killed while loading on T4 machines with limited RAM. ## Chat + Desktop - `unsloth start --continue` reopens your last agent session on the same model and settings. - Inkling 2 Mini no longer freezes laptops with 8 GB of VRAM and 16 GB of RAM after a few chats. - Thinking
4ce612ee14691da9a9ba4e17220e6582fcf56822.title: Inkling finetuning + perf fixes

4ced9b5daa264ea95664391c27928007cab43d9b.summary: arXiv:2611.05450v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.
4ced9b5daa264ea95664391c27928007cab43d9b.title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments

4d48dfa2cdaf0654914f1b1ee86ed3f78c1f3eec.summary: arXiv:2611.29793v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. We build a 640-task benchmark with three test sets (larger circuits, an unseen circuit family, an unseen Qiskit coding style) and a QuantumKatas regression probe, and we test the evaluator before training. Measurement counts miss every phase-only error; a surface rule-based translator solves two of three original splits (text substitution); a converter that executes the Qiskit input and maps the circuit solves all 640 tasks -- so the benchmark measures source-level translation, not whether a circuit can be ported after running it. No base model emits a valid CUDA-Q kernel zero-shot. On Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, LoRA reaches 83.9%, tying a 4-shot prompt (83.1%), but generalizes worse to unseen style (48.5% vs. 65.5%) and cuts QuantumKatas from 23.8% to 8.9%; on Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, LoRA beats the prompt overall (92.0% vs. 82.8%) and on unseen style (78.5% vs. 65.0%), and on the 1.5B model as well, so whether fine-tuning pays off depends on the base model, while the Qiskit regression appears in all three. Mixing two replay formats is the best mitigation trade-off (84.4% translation, Katas 21.5%). On 48 parametric functions that must become kernels with arguments -- where executing the input cannot yield a parametric kernel -- models reach up to 83%; on 27 real QED-C kernels, every model scores 0%. Language models can do source-level translation of simple parametric code, but not yet of real programs.
4d48dfa2cdaf0654914f1b1ee86ed3f78c1f3eec.title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study

4dbb07379a8488d4169cd6001fcd924edc459cc1.summary: arXiv:2611.29930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems let users without programming expertise query relational databases in natural language. Reinforcement learning has become the dominant way to train such systems, yet progress is still judged by a single number, execution accuracy, which counts correct queries but says nothing about which kinds of semantic error survive training. This paper develops a theoretical framework that examines text-to-SQL from the perspective of reward design. We introduce Reward Error Sensitivity, a measure of how strongly a reward function separates queries that contain a given error type from queries that do not, and prove a Reward Blindness theorem: when this sensitivity is zero, policy-gradient training carries no systematic signal for removing that error. Using fourteen published finegrained error signals for four text-to-SQL systems on the BIRD benchmark, we build error profiles and estimate sensitivities for common reward designs. Predicate and result-level errors are the most frequent, firing on up to 27 percent of queries, while structurally deep errors such as suboptimal joins persist at 5 to 12 percent. Each reward family has a distinct and predictable set of blind spots, and inexpensive database-level checks that need no language model calls detect 45 to 60 percent of semantic errors. Controlled training simulations confirm that executiononly reward leaves output-preserving errors untouched, whereas a signal-grounded reward removes them even when the detectors are noisy.
4dbb07379a8488d4169cd6001fcd924edc459cc1.title: Reward Blindness: A Theoretical Framework for Diagnosing Reinforcement Learning Reward Limitations in Text-to-SQL

4dec2de1c50c997cc97d06e7ea3050934baafbba.summary: arXiv:2611.29154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-video understanding requires systems to combine evidence from different videos for cross-video reasoning. Answering such questions involves two kinds of decisions. Observation decisions must adapt to each video's content, whereas cross-video judgments require relating evidence from different videos based on the question. Most existing agents make both kinds of decisions in one controller, whose context accumulates observations from every video. We separate them in MVAgent, a training-free Multi-Video Understanding Agent framework with one LocalAgent per video. Each LocalAgent plans observations of its own video and keeps a private observation history. A GlobalAgent coordinates cross-video reasoning by instructing the LocalAgents and combining their reports with joint observation. We evaluate MVAgent on CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, using three Qwen3.5 models of different sizes and GPT-6-sol. With Qwen3.5, our framework improves aggregate benchmark scores by 5.1 points on average over Single-pass inference with the same model and by 5.0 points over the strongest prior agent using the same model. With GPT-6-sol, the average gain over Single-pass inference with the same model is 4.3 points. On the same hardware, MVAgent also runs 1.8-2.7 times faster than prior agents of comparable size.
4dec2de1c50c997cc97d06e7ea3050934baafbba.title: MVAgent: Per-Video Agents under Global Coordination for Multi-Video Understanding

4e0584c3266b5d0f8c3c7a52f98644b0be4be42f.summary: arXiv:2611.28846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personal agents help users complete everyday work across digital applications. Many standard benchmarks assume that users provide sufficient information to solve a task. However, agents often encounter incomplete, distracting, or inconsistent information in practice. To systematically study agent inefficiency under such imperfect information, we introduce Efficient Action (EA)-Bench, which evaluates both tool calls and user interactions in work-related tasks. To our knowledge, it is the first benchmark to jointly evaluate tool-call efficiency and user-interaction efficiency under controlled missing, redundant, and conflicting information. We construct 63 base-task instances adapted from existing work-related benchmarks. To guide perturbation design and quantify task requirements, we represent workflows as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and examine node-level dependencies to identify where information can be withheld, contradicted, or supplemented with distractors. We use a two-stage validation process combining AI-assisted checks with expert screening to select 232 conditions from 792 initial candidates. We organize these tasks into Easy and Hard tracks by task complexity. Experiments show that imperfect information can reduce accuracy and increase tool-use and user-interaction costs. More concerning, several models obtain apparently correct outcomes by guessing user-specific values without confirmation, revealing potential execution unreliability in current models under imperfect user information.
4e0584c3266b5d0f8c3c7a52f98644b0be4be42f.title: EA-Bench: Measuring information and action efficiency under imperfect instructions

4e93173f6876a49c0c985f413f3e7d33d740bfc4.summary: arXiv:2611.29975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. However, as we show in this work, presenting an entire ruleset to a judge model---rather than asking it to judge one rule at a time---changes the way the model interprets the requirements, making it reach conclusions that conflict with its rule-by-rule judgments. We call this challenge multi-rule inconsistency and find that models are more lenient when judging rules embedded within the full ruleset than when judging rules separately. For example, we find that when a safety-critical rule prohibiting a model from pursuing objectives other than those it was given appears in a larger ruleset, all tested judge models are less likely to deem it violated. We examine several methods for reducing inconsistency, including prompting, consistency training using GRPO, and iterative rule refinement. As in human statutory interpretation, surrounding rules shape how a rule is interpreted. Unlike the legal setting, however, these interactions are currently happening implicitly inside the judge model's reasoning. We argue that multi-rule interactions must be measured and handled explicitly by ruleset designers to prevent undetected shifts in interpretation from causing downstream alignment failures.
4e93173f6876a49c0c985f413f3e7d33d740bfc4.title: Aligning Judge Models to Be Logically Consistent Multi-Rule Interpreters

4f56c8d7f4c84b2befff134d2f23a324dd20170a.summary: arXiv:2611.29590v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
4f56c8d7f4c84b2befff134d2f23a324dd20170a.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware

4f6dbf3841cd06766581040f96178d33d3caa1d4.summary: arXiv:2611.29028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.
4f6dbf3841cd06766581040f96178d33d3caa1d4.title: Do You Even Know What I Want? Improving LLMs Ability to Detect Hidden User Intent

4f7e088aba3047c2298a7b3401d978aecacb1ab2.summary: arXiv:2611.29395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decoding biological information from long, repetitive DNA remains challenging. Genomic language models (gLMs) often follow the conventional language-model pretrain-and-adapt paradigm. However, the lack of inherent semantic segmentation and prior rules makes hand-crafted tokenizers like k-mer and BPE suboptimal. We introduce context-aware \textbf{BQVAE} for scalar quantization of DNA and \textbf{BQDNA}, an autoregressive gLM supporting multi-head codebooks. Comprehensive experiments reveal that: (1) unique training dynamics of vector quantization in DNA space, including the importance of alignment between training corpus and downstream data. (2) superior performance of BQVAE over hand-crafted tokenizers and vanilla VQVAE. (3) remarkable cross-species generalization capability of BQDNA, which achieves state-of-the-art performance with merely 0.1B multi-species training for BQVAE and 1 epoch training on hg38 for BQDNA, outperforming gLMs pretrained with 10$\sim$100x more tokens. Our findings underscore the potential of learned vector quantization for genomic sequence representation. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/BQDNA
4f7e088aba3047c2298a7b3401d978aecacb1ab2.title: BQDNA: Multi-Head Binary Spherical Quantization for Genomic Sequence Modeling

4f81071420d385cdcb3ecfe56c52eee3e6e23965.summary: arXiv:2611.30207v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. We find that unsolved often means mislabelled: 74% of the tasks that a 9B base model never solves have a test that rejects correct fixes (a false negative), versus 20% of those it sometimes solves. We repair or remove such tasks, and the audited tasks that remain train better policies. At equal size and matched difficulty, models trained on them score 2.4 and 2.7 points higher on held-out tasks from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro than models trained on the original tasks, whereas simply dropping the never-solved tasks shows no such gain. We further find that wrong patches that pass (false positives) make up about a quarter of all passing patches, and that new tests that catch a quarter of them do not change held-out scores detectably. A pass rate shows whether a task yields reward, not whether that reward is right, so the reward labels themselves must be checked. To this end, we release SWE-Gym-Verified with its 1,087 audited tasks, every verdict with its executed evidence, our training sets, and the full audit pipeline.
4f81071420d385cdcb3ecfe56c52eee3e6e23965.title: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym

4fb02763f913e767aed73101dc83184c2afe93d2.summary: arXiv:2611.28565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jupyter notebooks support open-ended, multi-step assessments in which students build one logical flow across interdependent steps, combining code, written analysis, and generated outputs such as plots. These reflect authentic scientific practice but are hard to grade consistently, since students may make different yet equally valid choices at each step, so a later answer can only be judged in light of the choices a student made earlier. We present an LLM-based autograder for such flow-structured notebook questions. It generates a rubric from a reference solution, then applies a softening pass that relaxes criteria tied to the reference so legitimate alternative paths are not penalized. Each question group is graded in a single model call, so later answers are judged against the student's own earlier choices, using question-type tags and schema-constrained, low-temperature outputs. Evidence is scored multimodally: code, text, numerical outputs, and figures from code cells. We deployed the tool in a machine-learning course, integrated with Gradescope, with a pre-submission format check and prompt-injection defenses, and evaluate it both in that live course and against archived submissions graded by staff in earlier terms. We report agreement, cross-model variance, cost, student perceptions, and injection resilience. With low-temperature models, agreement with human scores is often strong, including on the open-ended items the design specifically targets, while run-to-run stability depends sharply on the model's temperature support.
4fb02763f913e767aed73101dc83184c2afe93d2.title: Beyond Unit Tests: Path-Aware Rubric-Guided LLM Autograding of Notebooks

4fde0fdfd4593ef28c8b531ed5c9f1c3f1c8ff6a.summary: arXiv:2611.10798v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hardware designs may be available only as gate-level netlists or input-output descriptions when the original register-transfer-level (RTL) design and documentation are not accessible. Low-level representations obscure word-level computation and its finite-width behavior. Recovering high-level RTL from such representations therefore helps engineers understand a circuit's functionality and enables RTL rewriting and resynthesis. A plausible function candidate is also insufficient unless the generated RTL is equivalent to the original circuit for all input combinations. In this paper, we present RTLREX, a large language model (LLM)-guided framework that coordinates domain-specific tools for function recovery, RTL generation, independent verification, and cost-guided rewriting. Independent verification establishes equivalence between the recovered RTL and the original circuit. The LLM uses tool feedback to select further analyses, revise RTL candidates, and propose syntax-cost reductions. Experiments on 30 benchmarks from Problem A of the ICCAD 2022 CAD Contest show that RTLREX recovers equivalent high-level RTL for all benchmarks, surpassing the state-of-the-art method WolFEx in recovery coverage. On benchmarks recovered by both methods, RTLREX reduces mean syntax cost by 20.5% relative to WolFEx. On complete truth-table benchmarks from the IWLS 2026 Contest, our framework reduces mean syntax cost by 95.7% relative to an LLM agent baseline on the benchmarks validated by both methods.
4fde0fdfd4593ef28c8b531ed5c9f1c3f1c8ff6a.title: RTLREX: LLM-Guided Framework for Exact High-Level RTL Recovery

4fe37f4d83c1675d9f01283e9afe7b0044752956.summary: arXiv:2611.29589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mid-generation abstention aims to stop an unpromising response before spending its remaining computation budget. Intermediate transformer states may help predict eventual correctness, but whether scalar summaries of their vocabulary predictions add useful evidence is less clear. We compare Tuned Lens entropy and divergence features with final-state and raw intermediate-state probes under matched, causal evaluation. Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, whereas scalar-only probes usually trail the final-state baseline. Scalar hybrids have positive exceptions, but their advantage over position-matched permutation controls is small. Cross-fitted residual comparisons further show that gains over a final-state probe need not require aligned scalar features. Actual stopping runs on two model sizes and two benchmarks reveal a separate accuracy--computation trade-off, with token savings overstating wall-time savings for scalar policies. The evidence supports a restricted empirical conclusion about these scalar features, not a general negative claim about intermediate representations.
4fe37f4d83c1675d9f01283e9afe7b0044752956.title: Scalar Tuned Lens Summaries Offer Limited Incremental Value for Mid-Generation Abstention

502c3582deb028a0260fe5996b02e028a072246f.summary: arXiv:2611.28706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills, yet maintaining them requires developers to connect revisions with changes in behavior and task outcomes. Existing workflows fragment evidence across versions, evaluation cases, and execution traces. We present SkillLens, an interactive human-LLM system for diagnosing and refining agent skills. A formative study with five developers and researchers identified challenges in prioritizing failures, reconstructing case-level evidence, and preserving context across revisions. SkillLens links performance changes, case transitions, skill diffs, invocation sequences, traces, and outputs in a recoverable workflow, while keeping model-generated explanations and refinements under human review. Through a between-subjects user study with 20 participants, we show that SkillLens supports developers in diagnosing and refining agent skills through a more usable and less demanding workflow than the baseline. These findings highlight the value of linking version comparisons, case-level evidence, and human-reviewed refinement across skill iterations.
502c3582deb028a0260fe5996b02e028a072246f.title: SkillLens: An Interactive Human-LLM System for Diagnosing and Refining Agent Skills

50b951e98c679f9daac898cbe34f0ed39a440163.summary: arXiv:2611.28194v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io
50b951e98c679f9daac898cbe34f0ed39a440163.title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds

50f07f04a757d3f65362fcc2304d4602c4e81307.summary: arXiv:2611.13000v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to base models, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks. Our work is open-sourced at https://github.com/lrm20011/ps_moe_open.
50f07f04a757d3f65362fcc2304d4602c4e81307.title: PhysMoE: Fast Spatial Grounding with Single-Token Coordinate Representation in Modality-Decoupled VLMs

513e1e974de6aee5589c7937e6c40d2af3412857.summary: arXiv:2611.25926v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7 percentage points and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.
513e1e974de6aee5589c7937e6c40d2af3412857.title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining

51b54d54c46c5f5c66a60fc2e3460e54ee8a2d61.summary: arXiv:2611.30873v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world text-to-SQL systems often face schema ambiguity, where a question can map to multiple plausible schema elements. To support downstream disambiguation, SQL generation systems should include diverse interpretations among their top-k predictions. However, large language models (LLMs) typically favor a single interpretation, producing highly skewed outputs. We propose Semantic-aware Logit Adjustment (SLA), a training-free decoding method that promotes diverse SQL generation by adjusting token logits based on semantic similarity between schema elements. Unlike prior approaches that rely on reasoning-intensive prompting or task-specific fine-tuning, SLA is efficient, model-agnostic, and easy to deploy. Experiments show that SLA consistently improves interpretation coverage over standard decoding and remains competitive with existing diversity-oriented methods at substantially lower inference cost.
51b54d54c46c5f5c66a60fc2e3460e54ee8a2d61.title: Semantic-aware Decoding for Diverse Text-to-SQL under Schema Ambiguity

51f9b95427646fe6d46f7730101a0810cc17a5ff.summary: arXiv:2506.14303v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep learning for surgical image analysis is constrained by limited data diversity, ethical restrictions, high acquisition costs, and the scarcity of accurately annotated bleeding datasets, making reliable bleeding localization particularly challenging. To address these limitations, we propose orGAN, a modular framework that generates realistic, fully annotated synthetic surgical bleeding images together with recoverable point-level supervision. To overcome the ethical and cost barriers of real surgical data, the pipeline is trained on silicone-based mimicking organs that reproduce tissue properties, using an enhanced StyleGAN3 generator coupled with Relational Positional Learning to embed bleeding coordinates, a Surgical Label Detection Algorithm to recover coordinate and mask labels, and a fine-tuned LaMa inpainting network to restore clean image-label pairs. To compensate for scarce annotations, Bleeding Alert Map (BAM) localization models are trained on a blend of synthetic and mimicking-organ images. The enhanced StyleGAN3 attains an Inception Score of 2.24, and the inpainting network preserves realism at a mean SSIM of 0.98. The blended model outperforms both single-source baselines, reaching a Dice coefficient of 0.635 on paired bleeding frames. With a stronger Pix2PixHD backbone, Dice rises to 0.893 with a centroid error of 6.3 pixels. On real Hamlyn surgical video, the blended model achieves a frame-level accuracy of 0.858 and a bleeding-frame detection rate of 0.998 on Hamlyn 2, where all 500 frames were annotated as bleeding-positive. These results show that combining realistic synthetic images with mimicking-organ data is an effective, ethical, and economical strategy for developing surgical AI under limited annotated data.
51f9b95427646fe6d46f7730101a0810cc17a5ff.title: orGAN: A Synthetic Data Augmentation Pipeline for Simultaneous Generation of Surgical Images and Ground Truth Labels

524bd15b45dbf9ed0c208b015b193771041b6cc9.summary: arXiv:2611.01970v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints. To address this, we reformulate the task as an explicit visual reasoning problem and propose HydroReasoner, a floodwater level reasoning framework designed for cloud-edge collaboration. HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. To address the scarcity of reasoning process annotations, we build a floodwater domain knowledge graph HydroKG and design a novel KG path reward. Through deterministic graph traversal over HydroKG, this reward supervises the model's reasoning process at a fine granularity, which improves both reasoning and generalization. For edge deployment, we apply 4-bit quantization to the model, cutting GPU memory usage by 57% and inference latency by 43% while out-of-domain accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points. We also propose a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism, which improves system safety and eases the computational load on the cloud. In addition, we build HydroLevel, a floodwater benchmark dataset of 3,000 images, for training and evaluating the model. Experimental results show that HydroReasoner achieves detection accuracy 4.0 and 13.6 percentage points higher than conventional vision baselines in the in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations respectively, with performance dropping by only 4.4 percentage points out of domain.
524bd15b45dbf9ed0c208b015b193771041b6cc9.title: Knowledge-Guided Floodwater Level Reasoning for Cloud-Edge Collaborative Monitoring

5254abe90d3d5d841f1516c50e1b8e50832cfaf9.summary: arXiv:2611.30891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aerosol forecasting requires integrating sparse ground observations and modeling meteorologically driven concentration evolution and spatial structure. However, analysis-initialized forecasts make limited explicit use of historical observations, while pointwise regression tends to smooth local variations and provides limited constraints on fine spatial structures. In this work, we propose AeroJEPA, a two-stage joint-embedding predictive framework for regional surface PM$_{2.5}$ forecasting. Specifically, Stage I fuses historical observations, model backgrounds, and meteorological information to predict an initial future state, meteorological conditions, and multi-scale structures. Morphology-guided encoding and joint-embedding predictive supervision support learning future spatial representations, supplementing concentration regression with structural constraints. Stage II uses predicted meteorology to guide state refinement and incorporates coarse- and fine-scale structures into state updates and decoding to generate the concentration field at a single future time step. Experiments show that AeroJEPA reduces gridded and independent-station RMSE by 17.23\% and 7.90\%, respectively, relative to PFGNet, while improving spatial consistency with analysis fields. In a 48 h recursive forecasting case study, AeroJEPA generally achieves lower RMSE and MAE than the numerical forecasts across the forecast period, indicating promising short- to medium-range forecasting performance.
5254abe90d3d5d841f1516c50e1b8e50832cfaf9.title: AeroJEPA: A Two-Stage Framework for Aerosol Forecasting with Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning

52731a9209ac98ed70ae77a5a6b60e4149d31392.summary: arXiv:2610.29467v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.
52731a9209ac98ed70ae77a5a6b60e4149d31392.title: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents

528f4d1c82bd22be46e5ae2b76175d8b8caab0c0.summary: arXiv:2611.25146v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.
528f4d1c82bd22be46e5ae2b76175d8b8caab0c0.title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work

52ea62913beb2b3abd454a37be714a2fbd666322.summary: arXiv:2611.29280v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.
52ea62913beb2b3abd454a37be714a2fbd666322.title: QASparse: Query-Adaptive Sparse Attention with Tailored Budgets and Tokens

52f5f75c9521b78c2f704fa8999e82ed76c6f896.summary: arXiv:2611.28834v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem, foundation models are increasingly deployed under AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS) schemes characterized by high technical opacity, technological concentration, and limited external auditing capability over governance, training, and internal operational processes. Under these conditions, traditional ethical oversight approaches that focus exclusively on corporate governance or on internal model inspection become insufficient to ensure effective control over AI systems deployed in real-world contexts. This work proposes a pragmatic operational assurance framework inspired by Zero-Trust principles from cybersecurity, which shifts effective auditing efforts toward the application layer, where risk acquires observable, contextualized, and operationally verifiable properties. The proposal articulates two complementary evaluation levels: a black-box evaluation aimed at characterizing general behaviors, vulnerabilities, and risky capabilities of foundation models through conversational scanning, and a grey-box evaluation focused on the operational contextualization of risk within the actual deployment environment of the audited application. The framework incorporates mechanisms to move from general, CVSS-inspired severity metrics toward contextualized operational risk assessments that take into account user profiles, industrial domains, and organizational knowledge. In addition, the proposal strengthens practical auditability through digitally signed explainability reports (signed XAI reports), designed to support verifiable traceability, continuous monitoring, and operational accountability in LLM-based sociotechnical systems.
52f5f75c9521b78c2f704fa8999e82ed76c6f896.title: Operational Assurance for LLM-Based Systems under Governance Opacity

52f83b1a07a69ba71e6fea6523d133a2b85ced41.summary: arXiv:2611.14083v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable
52f83b1a07a69ba71e6fea6523d133a2b85ced41.title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models

530e5283fa9babbf42ae583827683f02eefaddf1.summary: arXiv:2610.41790v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Average segmentation accuracy and model count do not reveal whether models fail on the same cases. We present CoFailMed, an audit of correlated failures in pretrained-encoder pools for medical segmentation. Across five 2D tasks, we evaluate 11 public pretrained encoders (a controlled sample, not a census) using frozen features and separately trained $1\times 1$ readouts with four seeds per encoder. Shared-checkpoint pairs have the highest mean per-case Dice correlation. An expanded 17-encoder analysis shows that distinct checkpoints within the same encoder family remain more correlated than cross-family pairs. At the pooled 33rd-percentile Dice threshold, four-member pools drawn from distinct encoders have mean effective sizes of 1.56-2.92, estimated from failure correlations in pools with enough failures and passes per member. In the primary pool, richer readouts and fine-tuning narrow the Dice-correlation gap between pairs sharing a checkpoint (or the DINOv2-B/S release) and all other pairs. Yet dependence between different encoders can increase, and fine-tuning does not consistently increase effective pool size at 33rd-percentile thresholds recomputed for each training recipe. A smaller between-group gap can coexist with greater dependence. Pool evaluation should therefore report absolute dependence and threshold-specific effective size alongside accuracy and nominal pool size. The CoFailMed release provides aligned per-case traces, analysis scripts and study code to reproduce the central audit results.
530e5283fa9babbf42ae583827683f02eefaddf1.title: Different Models, Shared Failures: Auditing Frozen-Encoder Pools for Medical Segmentation

53adcca4a59ceb1264b4877a41b0e64a7fa641f3.summary: arXiv:2611.30131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fetal brain diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a pivotal non-invasive tool for assessing the development of brain connectivity and microstructure. However, the prolonged acquisition times and complex sampling requirements render dMRI highly susceptible to unpredictable fetal motion. Existing motion correction methods typically process each dMRI volume independently and focus on inter-slice motion. Such strategies fail to utilize the coherent information between dMRI volumes along different diffusion directions and lack the ability to restore the intra-slice corruption. To address these limitations, we proposed iFeST, an iterative framework that combines frequency (k-space), spatial, and temporal (inter-slice) modeling for fetal brain dMRI motion correction. At each iteration, iFeST integrates information across diffusion directions into fiber orientation distributions (FODs). These distributions encode local fiber orientations within each voxel and serve as microstructural priors for intra-slice restoration and inter-slice alignment in the next iteration. To train the framework, we developed a fetal brain dMRI motion simulator that synthesizes compound motion artifacts from FODs. Evaluation on simulated datasets demonstrated that iFeST outperformed four inter-slice networks in motion estimation and three intra-slice networks in image restoration. Further validation on a real-world dataset confirmed significantly better volume reconstruction and FOD estimation than conventional pipelines. Overall, iFeST provides a learning-based framework for fetal dMRI motion correction, restoring motion-corrupted data and improving microstructural reconstruction for downstream diagnostic applications.
53adcca4a59ceb1264b4877a41b0e64a7fa641f3.title: iFeST: An Iterative Motion Correction Framework for Fetal Brain Diffusion MRI via Frequency-Spatial-Temporal Modeling

53f748d8abed6fee03d474f4628dfef96aa53854.summary: arXiv:2611.29811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: These notes describe how generative AI is now used to solve and to check research-level mathematics, with a focus on agents and their harnesses. For the proving agents Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos and the verification agent OSVerify, we explain the design principles, compare each with its base model, present case studies, and show how to use and contribute to them. We also briefly review the history of AI for mathematics and the community's reactions to it.

54040fee4e73e347ff254475893f4c68d26c49d1.summary: arXiv:2611.30410v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI models increasingly help to review papers, and many conferences and journals now require authors to state how they used AI. Does this AI-use statement change how an AI reviewer rates a paper, and could it change which papers are accepted? In a preliminary study, we varied only the AI-use statement of 150 ICLR 2027 submissions, in up to nine versions adapted from real statements: from no AI, through writing help and coding, to an AI research agent and an AI author. Six AI reviewers rated the versions: the decision model Jev and the language models Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 4 Argon. Across 23,652 reviews, we find that every reviewer rates papers lower on average when the statement says AI did all the work than under a statement of no AI use. The AI research agent statement lowers the rating significantly for Jev, Sonnet and Argon. We find no evidence of a disclosure bias for AI assistance: for writing help, coding and research help, no reviewer's rating differs significantly from its rating under a statement of no AI use. Whether the observed penalty changes which papers are accepted depends on more than the size of the penalty: on how finely and how consistently the reviewer separates the papers near the acceptance boundary, on whether the penalty is spread over all papers or concentrated on a few, and possibly on how many other papers disclose AI use.
54040fee4e73e347ff254475893f4c68d26c49d1.title: Disclosure Bias in AI Reviewers

545489afabaa0aec4cf1d630c124e1e1d6a70077.summary: arXiv:2611.18891v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.
545489afabaa0aec4cf1d630c124e1e1d6a70077.title: Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging
