f0d79b2d32bba3411c27c07fbcd527de824ffd87.summary: arXiv:2610.18001v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.
f0d79b2d32bba3411c27c07fbcd527de824ffd87.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models

f0dba3a6097fcd9082ae38fca556d423e0a98a41.summary: arXiv:2611.29651v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning data and chosen so that exposure disagreed with FPR alone or propensity alone, exposure named the first exploited pattern and its onset window in all six runs. Exploitation occurred only on hard prompts, where an accepted exploit gets a large group-normalized advantage. Auditing exposure before RL therefore identifies the loophole a policy will likely exploit first.
f0dba3a6097fcd9082ae38fca556d423e0a98a41.title: Which Loopholes Get Found? Predicting Reward Hacking of LLM Judges Before RL Training

f0e7469570081917dd5f68ece54b38988417d737.summary: arXiv:2611.29764v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given $K$ separately trained diffusion models, how should one sample from a $\beta_k$-weighted product of their terminal laws without jointly retraining the experts? Existing Feynman--Kac constructions provide many weighted stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with the correct target marginal. The consequential question is how to select useful proposal dynamics among them. We study an explicit family of weighted diffusions that realizes the same product-of-intermediate-experts trajectory. A scalar parameter $\lambda$ controls how strongly the proposal drift follows the composed expert score, while an additional Langevin component can be varied independently. Writing $B=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\beta_k>0$, we identify the distinguished choice $\lambda=1/B$. At this value, the aggregate squared-score term in the instantaneous Feynman--Kac log-weight rate cancels exactly. For positive expert exponents, the remaining score-disagreement contribution is non-positive. We call this structural cancellation Feynman--Kac reduction. Under bounded-divergence assumptions, it yields an upper bound on the instantaneous unnormalized log-weight rate for all $\lambda\leq 1/B$. For linear diffusion protocols with compactly supported expert data, $\lambda=1/B$ yields two-sided bounds at every nonterminal time, for exponents of either sign. A corresponding result holds for a single expert under the same divergence assumption. In these two-sided settings, the selected value is unique within the specified family in a universal worst-case sense. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and molecular sampling compare the analytically predicted stability with actual sampling quality, including instances in which parameter choices different from $\lambda=1/B$ perform better empirically.
f0e7469570081917dd5f68ece54b38988417d737.title: Selecting Stable Sampling Dynamics for Compositional Diffusion: A Feynman-Kac Weight Reduction

f1563d6fdc082d3f74bec2addd9329467b3e609b.summary: arXiv:2611.30047v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.
f1563d6fdc082d3f74bec2addd9329467b3e609b.title: RoboLiveMem: Is Robot Memory Solved When the World Does Not Wait?

f1ff1c03c68a42cac0a7c2c5ea741c1467356abe.summary: arXiv:2611.30200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI technologies and AI agents play increasingly important roles in human society, including in education, economics, and research. Adopting AI technologies can bring immediate, and sometimes tremendous, rewards such as through productivity boost, but they can also bring negative effects including but not limited to losses of job and training opportunities, and cognitive capability declines. Thus, it is important to investigate the optimal ways of adopting AI technologies without different traps. In this paper, we develop a general multi-agent Markov decision process (MDP) based reinforcement learning (RL or MARL) modeling framework for determining and analyzing optimal adoption of AI technologies. This framework can model the long-term dynamic effects of AI adoption, and lead to finding the optimal AI adoption strategies. In our modeling framework, the negative effects of AI adoption are modeled by undesirable state transitions or negative rewards in the MDPs. The proposed multi-agent RL MDPs incorporate both human agents and AI agents. The key idea of our models is that incorporating AI technologies may not only increase the immediate rewards for AI agents but also alter the states of the involved human and AI agents. In particular, we apply this framework to analyzing AI offloading leading to skill erosion, to analyzing optimal human resource structures for a firm adopting AI, and to analyzing the economic equilibria in the trading/employment among human and AI agents. Since the multi-agent MDP based RL technique is from control, machine learning and AI, this research is essentially using an AI technique to determine the optimal ways of adopting or co-existing with AI without traps.
f1ff1c03c68a42cac0a7c2c5ea741c1467356abe.title: Adopting AI Technologies without Traps: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework

f24d5a544b3cea6518ab3769bffac8f4346136c8.summary: arXiv:2611.20071v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.
f24d5a544b3cea6518ab3769bffac8f4346136c8.title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning

f2693e98691c15550da5e7055130422857d57472.summary: arXiv:2609.07131v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Proprietary LLM agents provide valuable specialized task-solving capabilities, yet limited service access may expose them to unauthorized capability theft. We investigate a previously underexplored strong-to-weak capability theft threat, where an adversary seeks to reconstruct a stronger proprietary agent's task-solving capabilities on a weaker, attacker-controlled agent. Our motivating study reveals a skill execution gap: even with access to the victim's authentic skills, a weaker agent fails to reproduce its task-solving performance, highlighting the execution asymmetry between stronger and weaker agents. Our key insight is that observable victim executions expose procedural knowledge that, when adapted to the execution capabilities of weaker agents, can enable capability reconstruction. We propose CapaTheft, which reconstructs capability-critical behaviors through workflow abstraction, differential gap diagnosis, and structured skill rewriting, without modifying the weaker agent's model, harness, or tools. Across 20 task scenarios comprising 600 instances and eight victim--attacker configurations, CapaTheft improves task pass rates by over 30% compared with direct skill reuse and recovers over 80% of the victim's capability advantage. Further evaluations demonstrate generalization to unseen instances, cross-system transferability, and the limited effectiveness of existing defenses. Our findings reveal that observable execution information, when adapted to the execution capabilities of weaker agents, can enable strong-to-weak task-solving capability theft without further victim access.
f2693e98691c15550da5e7055130422857d57472.title: From Service Access to Capability Theft: Cloning Task-Solving Capabilities of Proprietary LLM Agents onto Weak Open-Weight Agents

f32312c589a97efcde412935993d99e56ec317cf.summary: arXiv:2611.30087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning for protein engineering depends on functional measurements collected at screening scale, but the designs those measurements rank are deployed in processes that run elsewhere. Whether a miniaturized assay remains informative under the conditions of use is usually assumed rather than demonstrated. We describe an automated production and screening platform and test the transfer of its solution-phase metal-affinity measurements to immobilized rare-earth separation. Primary pKd-derived separation factors tracked those measured on covalently immobilized protein across 82 protein-metal-pair measurements from 35 proteins, with pairwise Spearman correlations of 0.878 to 0.923 (pooled Pearson $r$ = 0.836; Spearman $\rho$ = 0.869). Separation factors at a fixed metal pair are insensitive to the ordering shared across the lanthanide series, so these coefficients report protein-specific correspondence directly; permutation of protein identity confirms it, giving a mean scrambled correlation of 0.003 and, for the 17 proteins measured on all three pairs, $r$ = 0.917 against 0.001 ($p \approx 0.001$). Profiles compared as profiles behave differently. An independent comparison against published LAMBS profiles for the same protein backbones (417 proteins, 5,212 paired measurements) reproduced normalized raw elution at $r$ = 0.870, but reassigning protein identity still reached 0.840. High profile-level agreement across assay formats is largely attributable to metal preferences shared across the series rather than to protein identity. Transfer can be demonstrated, but the endpoint decides whether a correlation shows it: a pairwise contrast removes the shared ordering; a normalized profile retains it, and needs a null that reassigns protein identity.
f32312c589a97efcde412935993d99e56ec317cf.title: Correlated by Construction: Endpoint Choice and the Validation of Protein Screening

f39ecb0010048e83d7cab13c39c0ad7cbf0e0749.summary: arXiv:2611.30406v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion language models denoise a masked canvas, making them a natural setting for selective generation decisions such as answering, waiting, clarifying, or refusing. We introduce TAP-DiLM, which adds a typed policy variable to masked diffusion LMs, and study how this policy should be attached to the denoising process. Across BERT-base, MDLMOWT, LLaDA-8B, and Dream-7B, we compare shared-vocabulary slots, dedicated slot heads, and CLS-based external heads. The results reveal a clear interface-backbone interaction: dedicated heads provide robust policy learning across scales, while sharedvocabulary heads can be effective when the LM-head geometry is favorable. A simple LMhead sharpness probe predicts when sharedhead policy internalization is reliable, giving a practical diagnostic for interface selection. Causal clamp and slot-injection tests show that dedicated policy slots can influence body denoising through feedback, especially at 8B scale. Safety-refusal experiments further show that TAP-DiLM supports competitive typed refusal behavior when trained with diverse unsafe prompts.
f39ecb0010048e83d7cab13c39c0ad7cbf0e0749.title: TAP: Policy Interfaces for Diffusion Language Models

f3c5e6cb76b91844a8ad09e429a7aa1cc97e53da.summary: arXiv:2607.26075v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present IDP AutoOpt, an autonomous LLM agent that discovers high-performing configurations for intelligent document processing (IDP) pipelines. Tuning IDP prompts, models, OCR settings, and schemas jointly currently costs domain specialists 20 to 80+ person-hours per document type and does not scale as enterprises add document classes. IDP AutoOpt runs a closed loop: it scores a configuration on a small labeled set, diagnoses field-level errors, generates targeted edits, and re-evaluates, guided by human-authored domain skills that encode production expertise. Across extraction, classification, and packet-splitting tasks deployed in healthcare, marketing-intelligence, and financial-services settings, IDP AutoOpt matches or exceeds human-expert accuracy at equal or lower cost (on an extraction benchmark, 90.2% vs 81.6% at 4.6 x lower per-page cost), cutting configuration time from weeks to under two hours. We further show that agent LLM capability has a hard threshold below which optimization fails, and that curated domain skills outperform raw source-code access, which can degrade performance when provided without structure. We also share practical lessons on context management and variance mitigation. Requiring only a configurable pipeline, a scoring function, and a small labeled set, the approach extends beyond IDP to other enterprise AI systems, such as RAG and multi-agent workflows, where configuration bottlenecks deployment.
f3c5e6cb76b91844a8ad09e429a7aa1cc97e53da.title: IDP AutoOpt: Agent-Driven Optimization of Document Processing Pipeline Configurations

f41e96568ec9db1d4fb7b107010cc8c614a0beaf.summary: arXiv:2611.30494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.
f41e96568ec9db1d4fb7b107010cc8c614a0beaf.title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers

f51c4476b1c37ccbe13923844a4bfe03bda4ab05.summary: arXiv:2611.29847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Runtime guardrails protect mobile GUI agents by assessing each proposed action before execution, but existing guardrails rely on cloud hosted large multimodal models, exposing every screen to a remote server, including private information such as payments, messages, and medical records. We propose MobileGrail, an on-device deployable model that addresses both. It maintains a recurrent task state that retains only the evidence subsequent safety decisions depend on, so that authorization and execution progress persist beyond the short context. To intervene early while keeping the safety boundary precise, it learns two labels, unsafe and block: unsafe marks the action that commits a violation, whereas block may be issued at any step of an intervention window, which spans from the first action that the user's authorization no longer explains to the committing action itself. To support training, we build an environment of 32 applications whose backends verify the effect of every action, supplying verified labels for supervision and rewards for reinforcement learning to calibrate intervention timing. We also build MobileVeto, an offline benchmark of unsafe trajectories largely on held-out applications, each paired with a benign counterpart. On MobileVeto, MobileGrail built on Qwen3.5-2B intercepts 76.2% of violations, up from 64.5% for its prompted backbone, while reducing premature intervention from 58.6% to 5.2%, outperforming the cloud-based OS-Sentinel on both. We further conduct online evaluation on GhostEIBench, where MobileGrail guarding a Qwen3.8-27B agent reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while raising task completion from 48 to 58. Quantized to 4 bits, MobileGrail runs on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at a median latency of 4.7 s, comparable to the 5.1s of cloud-hosted Gemini 3.8 Flash.
f51c4476b1c37ccbe13923844a4bfe03bda4ab05.title: MobileGrail: Learning Compact Guardrails for On-Device deployable Mobile GUI Agent Safety

f5f5c7b19793743e9b619c786232f952e0e777a8.summary: arXiv:2611.29249v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: With the increasing adoption of geographic artificial intelligence, location encoders are widely used to map geographic coordinates to learned embeddings for tasks in Earth observation and geospatial modeling. Similar to map projections, location encoders can distort geographic space, that is, equal-distance displacements in different directions can result in unequal embedding changes. However, such distortion remains largely unexamined, and it can propagate into downstream applications. We adapt Tissot's indicatrix, a cartographic tool for map projection distortion, to characterize this distortion. At each location, we compare encoder outputs at equal distances in 32 directions and fit a tensor, represented by an ellipse, whose elongation (anisotropy) and orientation describe the local distortion. The fit requires only encoder outputs without access to model internals and is validated against references with known geometry. By applying the method to thirteen released checkpoints of five encoder families, we find that distortions vary across space and inherit the input geometry to varying degrees, closely in GeoCLIP with its Equal Earth input (anisotropy correlation of 0.88) and weakly or moderately in the other encoders. The distortion also affects the locations an encoder treats as neighbors. Within 1km of 20 query sites, the 40 nearest neighbors in geographic and embedding space overlap by a median of only 57.5--87.5% across the checkpoints, while the fitted ellipses select exactly the same embedding neighbors in 265 of 299 comparisons. These findings provide a geographic basis for assessing location encoders, and the accompanying eTissot package implements the methods for user-specified encoders.
f5f5c7b19793743e9b619c786232f952e0e777a8.title: Tissot indicatrix for location encoders: Characterizing local distortion in learned geographic embeddings

f60d43e178f70e453daf23a1fdc43137c04749d9.summary: arXiv:2602.13279v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid proliferation of rumors on social networks poses a significant threat to information integrity. While rumor dissemination forms complex structural patterns, existing detection methods often fail to capture the intricate interplay between textual coherence and propagation dynamics. Current approaches typically represent nodes through isolated textual embeddings, neglecting the semantic flow across the entire propagation path. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) as a structural augmentation layer for graph-based rumor detection. Moving beyond conventional methods, our framework employs LLMs to evaluate information subchains and strategically introduce a virtual node into the graph. This structural modification converts latent semantic patterns into explicit topological features, effectively capturing the textual coherence that has historically been inaccessible to Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). To ensure reliability, we develop a structured prompt framework that mitigates inherent biases in LLMs while maintaining robust graph learning performance. Furthermore, our proposed framework is model-agnostic, meaning it is not constrained to any specific graph learning algorithm or LLMs. Its plug-and-play nature allows for seamless integration with further fine-tuned LLMs and graph techniques in the future, potentially enhancing predictive performance without the need to modify original algorithms.
f60d43e178f70e453daf23a1fdc43137c04749d9.title: LLM-Enhanced Rumor Detection via Virtual Node Induced Edge Prediction

f653e6e2e7b9762fa21c0223c0dceed10031c90f.summary: arXiv:2611.29151v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Timely access to appropriate medical specialists remains a bottleneck in Bangladesh's healthcare system, as patients describe symptoms in informal Bangla rather than clinical terms, leading to ineffective referrals. This paper compares four model families for predicting medical specialties from Bangla patient narratives: six machine learning (ML) models using hybrid TF-IDF features, four deep learning (DL) models using Word2Vec embeddings trained on the corpus, four fine-tuned transformers, and five large language models (LLMs) evaluated zero-shot. From a corpus of 3798 patient records covering 20 specialties, we retained the five with the most records (Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, Gastroenterology) and split the resulting 2730 records 80:20 into training and test sets shared by all families. The best transformer was XLM-RoBERTa (86.26% accuracy, 86.21% macro-F1), the best ML model was SVM (84.98%, 84.92%), the best DL model was Bidirectional GRU (80.77%, 80.83%), and the best LLM was Gemini (90.29%, 90.15%). Holm-corrected paired McNemar tests show SVM significantly outperforming Bi-LSTM (adjusted p = 0.004), whereas the Gemini-versus-Grok gap does not survive correction (adjusted p = 0.104), and neither the strongest transformer versus the weakest LLM (Grok) nor SVM versus the strongest transformer reaches significance. A tuned classical model is thus statistically indistinguishable from the strongest transformer, so accuracy rankings alone should not be read as evidence of one family's superiority. The findings provide a comparative baseline for Bangla medical text classification.
f653e6e2e7b9762fa21c0223c0dceed10031c90f.title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs

f667c872efa876fbc4fc6815dd62fa7d30b4a03f.summary: arXiv:2608.18056v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hypothetical post-disaster urban environments may be partitioned into disjoint delay-tolerant-network (DTN) subregions under a thin-boundary information-isolation constraint, which severely limits cross-zone message delivery and makes centralized rerouting impractical. To address this, we propose Selective-Rerouter, a delayed-binding anonymous rerouting strategy for such partitioned environments. The scheme jointly exploits road occupancy and traffic speed for bottleneck detection, adaptively enlarges its upstream intervention window with congestion severity to include vehicles imminently approaching bottlenecks, and evaluates paths via horizon-aware fusion of live measurements and short-term forecasts, where only the prediction head of LSTAN-GERPE is fine-tuned with a path-ranking loss to preserve travel-time ordering, while a driver-aware scaling factor adjusts forecasts without altering live observations. Vehicles reroute only upon bottleneck encounters and keep K candidate routes. To assess performance under information isolation, we build a SUMO-based co-simulator coupling Selective-Rerouter on the intact side with a fixed DTN-UAV Forwarder inside each damaged corner. The forwarder consumes only scalar cost-announcements, performs no path-cost computation, and resolves civilian identities solely after bundles reach gateway buffers, thus acting as a testbed component rather than a novel DTN routing algorithm. Evaluations include standalone validation over undamaged districts, corner-level verification of cost-announcement-compliant bundle handoff, and four-corner tests that replace only the intact-side rerouting policy. Results show that hybrid live-forecast costing yields dominant travel-time gains. All experiments use discrete SUMO runs based on real-world urban road topology with artificially injected network partition damage, with no physical prototype.
f667c872efa876fbc4fc6815dd62fa7d30b4a03f.title: Selective-Rerouter: A Rerouting Strategy for Hypothetical Post-Disaster Urban Scenarios with a Thin-Boundary Co-Simulator

f677991c207d8735ff4e5bf120ca2be919578545.summary: arXiv:2611.28295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific information extraction (IE) is a fundamental component of AI for Science, transforming experimental knowledge embedded in scientific literature into structured and traceable data for evidence synthesis, scientific database construction, and data-driven discovery. However, critical experimental details are often distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and surrounding discussion, making them difficult to recover using conventional text-only extraction. Existing LLM-based and multimodal RAG pipelines typically rely on full-document context or coarse page-level retrieval, introducing substantial irrelevant evidence and high textual and visual token costs. We propose GERF, a Graph-based Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient, schema-guided multimodal scientific IE. GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.
f677991c207d8735ff4e5bf120ca2be919578545.title: GERF: A Token-Efficient Multimodal Retrieval Framework for Schema-Guided Scientific Information Extraction

f67cee1227ad461f7515d470a28b75c7aaf84bb9.summary: arXiv:2611.29327v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual token pruning can reduce the inference cost of vision language models, but its effectiveness depends on preserving complementary visual information under a limited token budget. A central challenge is to quantify the additional information a candidate token contributes beyond the retained set, a contribution that conventional scores based on attention or similarity struggle to capture directly. In this work, we revisit visual token pruning from the perspective of information gain and use mutual information to characterize the incremental value of candidate tokens. We further establish theoretically that frame potential serves as an effective surrogate for mutual information. Building on this observation, we propose FP-Prune, a training-free visual token pruning method that iteratively removes tokens with low information gain to preserve as much complementary visual information as possible. Experiments on three widely used VLMs and eight datasets demonstrate that FP-Prune outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and inference efficiency. Further analysis shows that the surrogate objective closely aligns with model performance. Our work provides theoretical grounding and an effective method for visual token pruning.
f67cee1227ad461f7515d470a28b75c7aaf84bb9.title: FP-Prune: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning from an Information Gain Perspective

f74d9ae95b67d80e9a051f199cec61483430e4d4.summary: arXiv:2605.23986v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-lived LLM agents maintain semantic views, such as fact records, profiles, and summaries, over a growing interaction history. Maintaining these views is a principal cost of agent memory: ingesting one conversation takes 15--53 minutes with leading memory systems, and most of this time lies on chains of dependent LLM calls that additional LLM capacity barely shortens. Because an LLM-generated view admits no delta rule, existing designs either serialize writes around revising views or give up fresh, reusable views. We present \textbf{MemForest}, which treats every view as a result derived from durable facts and recomputes it only from its children in a time-ordered tree. The dependency depth of view refresh then follows tree height rather than history length. Facts are extracted independently of existing memory, shared ancestors are refreshed once per batch, and independent views refresh in parallel. At query time, links from facts to trees recover details that compact views omit, and materialized interval views are reused for time-range aggregation. Against six released systems, MemForest builds memory \(4.7\times\) faster than EverMemOS on LongMemEval-S and \(8.8\times\) faster on LoCoMo. With Qwen3-30B, it matches EverMemOS on LoCoMo (84.1\%) and attains the highest LongMemEval-S accuracy (81.8\%).
f74d9ae95b67d80e9a051f199cec61483430e4d4.title: MemForest: Write-Efficient Agent Memory with Decoupled Extraction and Hierarchical View Maintenance

f75fae4b8e87b23d807146be2bb90b8464870e0d.summary: arXiv:2611.28314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.
f75fae4b8e87b23d807146be2bb90b8464870e0d.title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration

f772c0631868b4292fb8c3a1a41b178e48814df9.summary: arXiv:2611.30765v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects N in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on N. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all N objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget.
f772c0631868b4292fb8c3a1a41b178e48814df9.title: Object Count Generalization Is an Interface Problem: Warping a Frozen Skill Instead of Retraining It

f786a85c146aadd9480fa834db7123e683ee3345.summary: arXiv:2608.25091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-evolving Skill harnesses automatically rewrite an agent's procedural knowledge to improve efficiency, yet leave execution authority unconstrained. A Skill specifies how an agent should act, whereas a policy decides which requests may become physical actions; current Skill formats package procedure as markdown and scripts and leave authorization to the model. This gap is critical when a wrong invocation unlocks a door. We term the resulting failure Borrowed Authority: an inter-agent message pairs an instruction with an unverifiable permission claim, and the receiving Skill has no typed way to reject it. Across six open-weight receiver configurations (9,510 episodes), models execute 87% of unauthorized requests with no rule, 91% under a one-line rule, 25% when given the full policy in prose and a state-reading tool, and 18% behind a dedicated LLM checker. Failures concentrate on near misses (case variants, whitespace, wildcards, or just-expired readings), and where bare commands hesitate, an unverified claim displaces state checks. We propose Edge Skillguard, a typed invocation policy co-versioned with the actuator-owning Skill and enforced at the message boundary by a deterministic, fail-closed evaluator over leases, world state, and sensor freshness. Rather than using models as runtime filters, Edge Skillguard compiles prose rules offline behind an admission and operator-lattice tightening gate: across all six configurations and five policies, gated compilation yields verified guards (28/30 zero-shot, 30/30 after one feedback turn) and blocks 12/12 model-generated loosenings. On an edge testbed, Edge Skillguard admits 0/682 generated violations and 150/150 authorized requests at about 1 ms per decision, keeping invocation policy a fixed point outside the evolving harness's reach. Code and data: https://github.com/zhonghaozhan/edge-skillguard
f786a85c146aadd9480fa834db7123e683ee3345.title: Auto-Policy, not Auto-Skill: Compiled Agent Skills for the Physical World

f7880a7ccc385c0d303a896d90bf82ffd1ba7501.summary: arXiv:2608.00076v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal classifiers can achieve high accuracy while exploiting modality-specific shortcuts. Modality attribution quantifies the contributions of image and text, but does not by itself identify which input changes would alter a suspicious prediction. We introduce Counterfactual Modality Attribution (CMA), which connects modality-level contributions to explicit prediction-changing edits. CMA uses image and text diffusion priors to generate counterfactual references and constructs a two-player reference game whose Shapley--Taylor decomposition separates image, text, and interaction contributions. The method requires class-score queries but no model gradients. Attribution profiles are compared with a reference population to prioritize predictions with atypical modality reliance for review, while counterfactual edits expose localized evidence for inspection. On controlled image- and text-biased classifiers, CMA identifies the ground truth dominant modality for all evaluated inputs. On planted-shortcut benchmarks, it achieves shortcut-reliance detection AUROCs of 0.987 on Synthetic MNIST and 1.000 on OpenI, with image-shortcut localization IoUs of 0.97 and 0.84, respectively. An API experiment demonstrates applicability to a native multimodal language model with scored answer choices. CMA enables predictions to be screened by modality reliance and investigated through explicit counterfactual edits.
f7880a7ccc385c0d303a896d90bf82ffd1ba7501.title: Which Modality Decides? Counterfactual Modality Attribution for Multimodal Classifiers

f7988fd73c94421562b7b31a1ff9bdcb976d73d0.summary: arXiv:2605.24743v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While LLMs excel at single-turn generation, they struggle with long-horizon, multi-turn interactions. Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers a scalable approach, yet its performance hinges on the availability and quality of multi-turn trajectory data. A common remedy is to augment training with synthetic trajectories generated by LLMs or simulators, but synthetic data is highly heterogeneous in quality, and naively treating all trajectories as equally informative can degrade performance. We propose BOOST, a bilevel optimization framework where the inner level trains the LLM on reweighted data and the outer level trains a lightweight reweighting head on held-out real validation tasks, assigning continuous trajectory-level weights without requiring an external judge. To ground this approach, we derive a PAC-Bayesian bound revealing a three-way trade-off: synthetic data increases diversity but risks task-shift, while concentrating weight on high-quality trajectories improves empirical performance at the cost of effective sample size. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms multiple baselines. Analysis reveals it upweights synthetic trajectories that align with the real data distribution and exhibit higher qualitative merit.
f7988fd73c94421562b7b31a1ff9bdcb976d73d0.title: Bilevel Optimization of Synthetic Trajectories for Multi-Turn LLM Fine-Tuning

f7dd1873faacd3509c85f4547a1bc47d6a884d43.summary: opencode-pty 0.5.2 (protocol 8) from packages/process-daemon, published to npm as @opencode/pty@0.5.2.
f7dd1873faacd3509c85f4547a1bc47d6a884d43.title: process-daemon v0.5.2

f7e1aa32e7c1768e020dfcb9e31c523858c85a99.summary: arXiv:2610.41835v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop ReuScope, a protocol for auditing data reuse and evaluation sensitivity, using Capsule Vision 2024 as a case study. It combines measurements of data relationships with two comparisons: changing the evaluation population while holding predictions fixed, and changing training data while holding evaluation fixed. Byte-identical files cross the public training-validation boundary, and all 41 Kvasir-Capsule recordings that contribute frames occur in both partitions. Shared source recordings establish cross-split overlap; missing cross-recording patient identifiers prevent counting unique shared patients. Across ten paired seeds, removing all training rows attributed to Kvasir-Capsule, plus five rows from other sources flagged as near-matches to it, lowers public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%. Evaluating the same fitted models on the validation rows of the other sources reverses the comparison: removal improves balanced accuracy by 1.38 percentage points. The public-validation drop measures sensitivity to source removal, not an amount of leakage-induced inflation. Matched controls show that sample size and class counts alone do not explain the observed score differences. An exploratory experiment removes the training neighbors of validation frames that have close training matches, or equally many distant training rows, and yields a difference-in-differences estimate, relative to matched unflagged frames, of -0.355 percentage points in true-class probability; the paired-t interval for accuracy spans zero. The resulting procedure distinguishes observed reuse from conditional performance sensitivity and specifies the population, class support and uncertainty unit for each conclusion.
f7e1aa32e7c1768e020dfcb9e31c523858c85a99.title: ReuScope: Auditing Data Reuse and Evaluation Sensitivity in Capsule Vision 2024

f7f2e281af036cd846a2b7af973ea0b63ac5c052.summary: arXiv:2604.06132v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for multi-step workflows in real-world software environments. However, existing agent benchmarks are limited by trajectory-opaque grading, underspecified safety and robustness evaluation, and narrow coverage of modalities and interaction paradigms. We introduce Claw-Eval, an end-to-end evaluation suite addressing these gaps with 300 human-verified tasks spanning 9 categories across three groups: general service orchestration, multimodal perception and interaction, and multi-turn professional dialogue. To enable trajectory-aware grading, each run is recorded through three independent evidence channels: execution traces, audit logs, and environment snapshots, yielding 2,159 fine-grained rubric items. The scoring protocol evaluates Completion, Safety, and Robustness, with Average Score, Pass@k, and Pass^k across three trials to distinguish genuine capability from lucky outcomes. Experiments on 14 frontier models show that: (1) Trajectory-opaque evaluation is systematically unreliable, missing 44% of safety violations and 13% of robustness failures detected by our framework. (2) Capability does not imply consistency, with Pass@3 remaining stable under error injection while Pass^3 dropping by up to 24 percentage points. (3) Agent capability is strongly multi-dimensional, with model rankings varying across task groups and metrics, indicating that our heterogeneous evaluation coverage is essential. Claw-Eval highlights directions for developing agents that are not only capable but reliably deployable.
f7f2e281af036cd846a2b7af973ea0b63ac5c052.title: Claw-Eval: Towards Trustworthy Evaluation of Autonomous Agents

f81dd84aedadd9b503edb75dfa91de657f01c9ee.summary: arXiv:2611.29243v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.
f81dd84aedadd9b503edb75dfa91de657f01c9ee.title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents

f87f9ff8b0fe11355b2e39b18509dbeb75cb5cca.summary: arXiv:2611.28153v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development, yet our understanding of how they generate code remains critically underdeveloped. We address this gap by triangulating evidence across three layers. Longitudinally, autonomous agent-attributed code is statistically indistinguishable from human code under a semantic modification definition (HR = 1.019, p = 0.490), yet attracts disproportionately corrective modifications in production (49.1% vs 37.9% human baseline). This finding demands a causal explanation. Empirically, existing benchmarks overestimate LLM capabilities: models that achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks attain only 24 to 35% on real-world class-level code. Behaviourally, detection systems reveal puzzling asymmetries: GPT-3.5 is far more detectable than modern models (AUC-ROC = 0.96, a 27-point gap), even though modern models produce mutually similar code structures; yet no single feature reliably distinguishes AI-generated from human code at the class level, and the leading commercial detector achieves only 15 to 64% recall. Together, these findings raise a question that empirical studies cannot answer: why do LLMs generate code with these properties? This thesis proposes mechanistic interpretability, a causal token-level circuit tracing, as the bridge between empirical observation and principled correction. By identifying the transformer circuits responsible for detectable stylistic signatures, hallucination patterns, and systematic defects, we aim to drive an agentic repair framework that intervenes at the causal source of defects rather than patching surface symptoms.
f87f9ff8b0fe11355b2e39b18509dbeb75cb5cca.title: From Observation to Explanation: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM-Generated Code for Principled Repair

f8b000664cd11c16ef83c994f78de3f75a42c23d.summary: arXiv:2611.28968v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hospitals often update a deployed risk model by adding a data source, such as laboratory results, that only some patients have. Work on safe model updates assumes fixed inputs and so ignores patients who lack the new data. The update has no new measurements for them, yet their rank can change, and a sick patient not yet tested can drop off an alert list. We split rank-based compatibility by data availability and pair it with error correction and alert-list effects. We compared each update with ordinary retraining on the old inputs, predicting ICU admission or death and hospital admission, on 78,475 emergency department visits from MC-MED and, in a pre-registered replication, 100,000 stays from MIMIC-IV-ED at a second hospital. Radiograph report text gave no detectable gain and almost no extra re-ranking. Laboratory results improved prediction but, at both hospitals and with linear or tree models, pushed patients without labs down alert lists; linear updates also reshuffled them more than retraining did, without ranking them better. A top-20% admission list caught 4.2% of admitted patients without labs after the update, against 18.8% after retraining (second hospital: 4.9% against 22.6%), while catching more patients overall. This held for list sizes from 5% to 50% and in every patient group we checked, despite better measured calibration. Separate alert thresholds for patients with and without labs restored most or all of their catch rate at both hospitals at almost no cost. Teams should check these patients before deploying such an update.
f8b000664cd11c16ef83c994f78de3f75a42c23d.title: Who Gets Re-ranked When a Clinical Model Gains New Data?

f8cdee5e54e69b79cb16c1ef48b864d9cc9b77b2.summary: arXiv:2611.28135v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large vision-language models can extract personally identifiable information from images, making privacy protection essential for their deployment in perception-oriented tasks. Existing targeted fine-tuning and model-editing methods usually suppress sensitive answers by aligning the model toward safe responses. In this paper, we show that such protection can be illusory: although the fine-tuned model refuses to disclose private information under normal decoding, privacy leakage still occurs in sentence completion scenarios. This indicates that existing algorithms only change the model's output distribution, but the model still retains the ability to perceive private information. Private information therefore still remains inside the model. To address this problem, we propose Visual Intrinsic Privacy Erasure (VIPE), which targets privacy-related visual representations to weaken the model's ability to perceive sensitive information. VIPE constructs paired privacy-sensitive and privacy-masked images, uses their internal feature residuals to identify privacy-related visual components, and suppresses these components before they are perceived by the model. To preserve benign visual representations, the erasure objective projects feature differences onto a relaxed benign subspace and adaptively controls the erasure strength. VIPE compels the model to ignore the extraction of sensitive information in the visual representation space, thereby blocking the source of privacy leakage more fundamentally rather than merely altering the model's output distribution. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and LLaVA-OneVision show that VIPE substantially alleviates prefix-triggered privacy leakage while maintaining competitive utility on general visual-language benchmarks.
f8cdee5e54e69b79cb16c1ef48b864d9cc9b77b2.title: Beyond Output Suppression: Mitigating Privacy Risks in LVLMs via Visual Intrinsic Privacy Erasure

f901eb7b293aaf55564d4339afa9c82af00a98b3.summary: arXiv:2606.16620v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Inference-time scaling has become the dominant lever for improving language-model reasoning, but existing methods often derive rollout diversity from a single source: stochastic token-level sampling. We identify a second, fully \emph{deterministic} and \emph{complementary} axis: the layer span $L$ at which a frozen model's top decoder layers are recursively re-applied at high-uncertainty tokens. Different choices of $L$ produce distinct rollouts that solve different subsets of problems, with no stochasticity. We instantiate this axis through \emph{Entropy-Gated Latent Recursion} (EGLR), a training-free decoding procedure that, combined with temperature sampling, turns a single-axis rollout pool into an $L\!\times\!T$ Cartesian sampling space at almost the same per-rollout cost. Across $8$ instruction-tuned models and $6$ math benchmarks, majority voting over the $L$ axis matches or improves on greedy decoding in nearly all settings and outperforms FLOP-matched beam search, and the gains carry over to a code benchmark. On MATH-500, the oracle ceiling of the joint pool exceeds that of either axis alone by $8$ to $10$ points. In a preliminary study, using the pool for GRPO rollouts with importance-sampling correction improves over standard GRPO. The code is available at \href{https://github.com/spotai-mbzuai/neurips26-eglr}{https://github.com/spotai-mbzuai/eglr}.
f901eb7b293aaf55564d4339afa9c82af00a98b3.title: Entropy-Gated Latent Recursion

f975318429d918175b829a693f75424ca21e5a33.summary: arXiv:2611.31165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When should additional reasoning or verification replace a majority-vote answer? We call such a replacement an override. We examine two obstacles: the availability of correct alternatives and the reliability of methods that produce or select them. We compare additional reasoning, executed programs, and cross-model reasoning on 150 competition-mathematics questions with three open reasoning models. Starting from a majority vote over 16 responses, we measure how often overrides occur and how many errors they correct or introduce across agreement thresholds. When the vote is incorrect, the correct answer is often absent from the original responses. Additional same-model reasoning rarely overrides, while executed programs correct more errors than they introduce at every evaluated threshold. Cross-model overrides improve some weaker baselines but do not establish an advantage over the more accurate model alone, even with only eight standalone responses. Stricter agreement reduces how often overrides occur but does not consistently increase the fraction that correct errors. At the strictest thresholds, overrides occur on few distinct questions, limiting conclusions about their reliability.
f975318429d918175b829a693f75424ca21e5a33.title: When Does Overriding the Majority Vote Help?

f9b659f87814a917b63b2dc2b3ccebf0b017da4e.summary: arXiv:2611.29566v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Test-time compute has become an important paradigm in computer vision and language modeling, where additional computation at inference time enables models to explore multiple candidate solutions and select or refine the most reliable one. However, time series forecasting models typically produce predictions through a single forward pass, leaving them vulnerable to distribution shifts and non-stationarity that frequently arise in real-world temporal data. We propose Time Test Compute for Time Series (TTC4TS), an architecture-agnostic framework that improves the predictive performance of frozen forecasting models at inference time. Given a pretrained backbone, the generator produces multiple candidate forecast trajectories using augmentation, retrieval, adapter. The synthesizer then selects or combines these candidates using aggregation, classification, or candidate-scoring and ranking methods to produce the final forecast. By increasing the number of candidates, TTC4TS scales test-time compute without retraining the forecasting backbone. Beyond improving point-forecast accuracy, TTC4TS can exploit candidate forecasts for uncertainty quantification, which supports improved interval forecasts. We also theoretically analyze when additional test-time computation improves forecasting. Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones demonstrate consistent gains in accuracy and calibration. Code is provided in https://github.com/Anoise/TTC4TS.
f9b659f87814a917b63b2dc2b3ccebf0b017da4e.title: Think Before You Forecast: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Time Series Forecasting

fa58ef34914a72bd55e7f913401f8e0c92bb885e.summary: arXiv:2608.18339v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot capabilities yet remain sensitive to real-world distribution shifts. Although significant efforts are devoted to adapting VLMs at test time, they rely heavily on noisy pseudo-labels predicted from cross-modal embedding similarities during inference, which are unreliable under distribution shifts and mislead the adaptation. Moreover, existing methods largely overlook the critical relational structures across different modalities during test-time adaptation, whose supervision signals remain surprisingly robust under distribution shifts. In this work, we aim to jointly align the cross-modal semantics and intra-modal relational structures across modalities at test time to improve VLM adaptation. At the inference stage, we formulate the zero-shot image classification task as a cross-modal alignment problem via a Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) formulation, which considers both cross-modal semantics and intra-modal structures to generate robust pseudo-labels. At the adaptation stage, we propose a multi-level InfoNCE loss to leverage both the semantical and relational alignment supervision from the inference stage, empowering fine-grained adaptation of VLMs under distribution shifts with additional structural consistency. Finally, we bridge the inference and adaptation stages of our method by proving a mathematical equivalence between their objective functions, thereby revealing the mutual benefits of these two stages from a theoretical perspective. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our methods, outperforming the best-performing methods by up to 3% while maintaining a superior balance between effectiveness and efficiency.
fa58ef34914a72bd55e7f913401f8e0c92bb885e.title: From Inference to Adaptation: Vision-Language Model Test-Time Adaptation via a Unified Optimal Transport View

fa6c6b9ff1a8239b40148554a9a176675355f79a.summary: arXiv:2611.29132v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.
fa6c6b9ff1a8239b40148554a9a176675355f79a.title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery

faa4312742be2bb7d40cf9aa512ae03a18b75eb1.summary: arXiv:2606.19399v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-based formal provers often collapse the verifier's output into a pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that feeds what Lean reports (error messages with their position, verified partial proofs, and remaining goals) back into proof search. Phase 1 samples N whole proofs; Phase 2 searches a tree of verified partial proofs with a Tactician, automated step repair, a Critic that ranks states and allocates the budget, and a Retriever. On miniF2F test, VERITAS solves 86.9% with Claude Haiku 5.5 and 82.8% with GPT-6 Luna, against 71.7% and 61.1% for Best-of-5 sampling, and solves more theorems than three re-implemented feedback baselines at a third to a half of their search cost. We also evaluate on 55 combinatorics problems of CombiBench and release code and run logs at https://github.com/CoderDoge1108/VERITAS.
faa4312742be2bb7d40cf9aa512ae03a18b75eb1.title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving

faf42cd7f7101279a35fdadcda0d2e3dc72bdc94.summary: arXiv:2611.29727v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic software development pipelines with frozen prompts can repeat the same mistakes across pull requests (PRs), yet ungoverned additions to instruction files grow without bound and do not generally improve task success. We present a retrospective loop for a four-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline in which a Retrospective agent proposes edits to learned rules every ten PRs and a Notary admits, merges, or rejects them while recording each decision in a provenance ledger. In a pre-registered study of 880 PRs on two Python repositories, the loop ran end to end and the Notary admitted 55 of 89 proposals, rejecting 8 that cited nonexistent evidence. However, held-out review comments and hidden-test resolution did not improve after ten retrospectives. Tracing each step of the loop, we found that sparse review signal (0.45 comments/PR) left little to learn from and that rules admitted on their stated evidence did not show measurable held-out effects. We derive six lessons and argue that governed loops should admit and retire every learned rule as a testable hypothesis.
faf42cd7f7101279a35fdadcda0d2e3dc72bdc94.title: Admitted Is Not Effective: Lessons from a Notary-Gated Retrospective Loop in an Agentic Pipeline

fb34f3154d5f1d8c93894e31c4e764d7151695f5.summary: arXiv:2611.28978v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.
fb34f3154d5f1d8c93894e31c4e764d7151695f5.title: World Models for Ocean Engineering: A Critical Review of Maritime Autonomy, Adaptive Latent Prediction, Digital Twins, and Biodiversity Monitoring

fb77233b70ba317dbab69ea58128224d1c314184.summary: arXiv:2609.29674v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sequential task updates are fundamental to continual learning, but their recency bias can impose a lasting performance cost. We study this cost in an overparameterized linear-regression model with i.i.d. task sampling. We prove that distribution-level forgetting and population loss converge to the same stationary limit. We quantify the additional loss incurred by sequential exact fitting, or the sequential price. If all nonzero eigenvalues of all task curvature matrices equal the same constant, the stationary loss is exactly twice the joint-training optimum. We further analyze fixed-strength elastic weight consolidation (EWC) under general task curvatures and characterize its stationary sequential price at every regularization strength. Under strong regularization, the price decays inversely with EWC strength while the number of tasks sufficient to reduce the mean-square effect of initialization by a fixed factor grows proportionally. Real Jester user ratings, with a natural encoding and training procedure, satisfy our theoretical assumptions.
fb77233b70ba317dbab69ea58128224d1c314184.title: The Sequential Price of Continual Learning

fb7beb2a73b742f82eae3ed85f49b0435c7430e2.summary: arXiv:2610.09221v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Flow and diffusion models suffer from slow inference due to computationally expensive numerical integration. Distillation provides a promising way for a student model to learn from a teacher's dynamics, enabling one-step or few-step generation. However, existing methods often depend on curated distillation datasets, orchestration of multiple objectives, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, which complicate model training and scaling. In this work, we propose Consistent Distribution Matching, a simulation-free and data-free distillation method for accelerating diffusion and flow models while preserving strong generative capacity of the teacher model. Our key insight is to unify sample generation and score estimation with one student network, which greatly simplifies the distribution matching distillation pipeline. Thus, our framework uses only two models, a frozen teacher and a trainable student, and optimizes one objective. We prove that minimizing our objective indicates Wasserstein convergence of the student flow-map pushforwards to the teacher marginals. On ImageNet 256$\times$256, our method attains an FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37, surpassing the state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data. On text-to-image distillation tasks, our method also enable fast high-fidelity generation with no image data required. Our code code and model are available at https://consistentdmd.github.io/.
fb7beb2a73b742f82eae3ed85f49b0435c7430e2.title: Consistent Distribution Matching for Data-Free Diffusion Distillation

fba4d35488a1603973f6fc7735f0ac308e96206b.summary: arXiv:2603.10701v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) aims to recover the speech of a specified speaker from a multi-talker mixture using a short enrollment utterance from that speaker. Real conversational applications require both high extraction quality and low-latency inference across complex mixture conditions. Existing generative TSE approaches improve speech fidelity, but diffusion and flow-based models usually rely on multi-step sampling. One-step variants reduce iterative inference cost, yet often require estimating a trajectory coordinate related to the mixing ratio, introducing an additional dependency. We propose AlphaFlowTSE, which formulates TSE as finite-interval transport from the observed mixture to clean target speech. AlphaFlowTSE learns a conditional mean velocity along a mixture-to-target trajectory and uses a JVP-free AlphaFlow objective that combines local trajectory matching with interval-consistent teacher--student supervision. This parameterization supports predictor-free inference while remaining compatible with an optional MR-enabled configuration. At separator NFE$=1$, the MR-enabled configuration attains the highest PESQ, ESTOI, and SI-SDR among the compared one-step systems on Libri2Mix; under predictor-free inference on REAL-T PRIMARY, AlphaFlowTSE yields lower downstream ASR error rates and higher target-speaker similarity.
fba4d35488a1603973f6fc7735f0ac308e96206b.title: AlphaFlowTSE: One-Step Generative Target Speaker Extraction via Conditional AlphaFlow

fbf0edcb3fb7d778cfbb466f72549048d0a85195.summary: arXiv:2611.15309v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.
fbf0edcb3fb7d778cfbb466f72549048d0a85195.title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution

fc00fc1c9b234c28286d9cfd0b33cccf083208e3.summary: arXiv:2611.29467v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.
fc00fc1c9b234c28286d9cfd0b33cccf083208e3.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents

fc2187aaaa0745df20c6742689afa18b9cbf089e.summary: arXiv:2511.14112v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automatic ICD coding from clinical text is a critical task in medical NLP but remains hindered by the extreme long-tail distribution of diagnostic codes. Thousands of rare and zero-shot ICD codes are severely underrepresented in datasets like MIMIC-III, leading to low macro-F1 scores. In this work, we propose a data-centric framework that generates high-quality synthetic discharge summaries to mitigate this imbalance. Our method constructs realistic multi-label code sets anchored on rare codes by leveraging real-world co-occurrence patterns, ICD descriptions, synonyms, taxonomy, and similar clinical notes. Using these structured prompts, we generate 90,000 synthetic notes covering 7,902 ICD codes, significantly expanding the training distribution. We fine-tune two state-of-the-art transformer-based models, PLM-ICD and GKI-ICD, on both the original and extended datasets. Experiments show that our approach modestly improves macro-F1 while maintaining strong micro-F1, outperforming prior SOTA. While the gain may seem marginal relative to the computational cost, our results demonstrate that carefully crafted synthetic data can enhance equity in long-tail ICD code prediction.
fc2187aaaa0745df20c6742689afa18b9cbf089e.title: Synthetic Clinical Notes for Rare ICD Codes: A Data-Centric Framework for Long-Tail Medical Coding

fc8805afe15cb2d617a2cd2151306f62fda0505d.summary: arXiv:2611.28517v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Digital twins of agent networks need to flag unreliable forecasts and help users choose interventions. Both decisions depend on what happens over several steps: an error can spread through the network, and an edit whose trajectory is easy to predict may still yield a poor collective outcome. We ask when information about error propagation improves failure detection and whether a learned twin can select effective network edits despite imperfect forecasts. We propose Propagation-Aware Validation for Networked Digital Twins (PAV-Twin). Its monitor combines Jacobian-based propagation features with recent errors and ensemble disagreement to estimate the risk that a forecast exceeds an error threshold. Its planner simulates each candidate edit and ranks the edits by their predicted collective outcomes. In simulations, the monitor gained 0.13 in area under the precision-recall curve on larger oscillator networks with familiar topologies and 0.09 on larger networks with held-out topologies, relative to a graph baseline without propagation features. Gains were small in contractive consensus. Giving the graph baseline the same features narrowed the gap. In a separate planning study, ensemble simulation recovered about 99% of the possible improvement over random intervention selection in oscillators and nearly all of it in consensus. With a simplified oscillator twin, selecting by predicted outcome also gave lower regret than selecting by trajectory fidelity. These results show when propagation features help flag unreliable forecasts and why the quality of intervention choices should be measured directly.
fc8805afe15cb2d617a2cd2151306f62fda0505d.title: Digital Twins for Multi-Agent Systems: When to Trust, What to Change
